name: Classic-Style Test 6
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Glaciologist: The Vellin Glacier has retreated nearly two kilometers over the past century, and many visitors assume that the retreat began with the warming of recent decades. But survey markers left by mapmakers in the 1880s show that the glacier’s front was already pulling back then, long before that warming started. Recent warming, therefore, cannot be the whole explanation for the glacier’s retreat, even if it has sped the retreat up.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the glaciologist’s argument?
choices: The front of the Vellin Glacier was already pulling back in the 1880s, long before recent warming began.
Recent warming does not by itself account for the Vellin Glacier’s retreat over the past century.
Recent warming has increased the rate at which the Vellin Glacier is retreating.
The Vellin Glacier has retreated nearly two kilometers over the course of the past century.
Many visitors are mistaken in believing that the Vellin Glacier is retreating at all.
questions.explanation: The word “therefore” marks the point everything else supports: recent warming cannot be the whole explanation for the retreat, which (B) restates. (C) is tempting, but the glaciologist only concedes that warming may have sped things up (“even if”); that is not asserted, let alone argued for. (A) is the evidence, and (E) distorts the visitors’ view, which is about when the retreat began, not whether it is happening.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Recent warming cannot be the whole explanation for the Vellin Glacier’s retreat.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mapmakers’ markers show the front was already pulling back in the 1880s, before recent warming started.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is background: the glacier retreated and visitors blame recent warming. The 1880s markers are the evidence. “Therefore” flags the point: warming isn’t the whole story. It’s like saying: the leak started before the new tenant moved in, so the new tenant can’t be the whole reason the ceiling is damaged. The “even if” clause is a concession, not a claim the speaker argues for.

choices.note: This is the premise. The survey markers prove it, and it in turn proves the conclusion. It sits in the middle of the support structure, not at the top.
CORRECT. “Cannot be the whole explanation” means the same thing as “does not by itself account for.” It’s what “therefore” marks, and the 1880s evidence is there to support it.

Tempting, because it appears in the last sentence. But read the words: “even if it has sped the retreat up.” The glaciologist allows that this might be true without asserting it. A concession isn’t the conclusion.
Background. It sets the scene and nobody disputes it. Nothing in the argument is offered to prove it.
Distortion. The visitors think the glacier is retreating, and the glaciologist agrees. The disagreement is about when the retreat began and what caused it.

questions.stimulus: Blogger: Audiologists have exaggerated the danger that loud music poses to hearing. They warn that people who are regularly exposed to loud music face an increased risk of permanent hearing loss. But my uncle has played drums in loud nightclubs several nights a week for forty years, and a hearing test last month found his hearing to be normal for his age.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the blogger’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to specify how much exposure to loud music would be needed before hearing loss became likely
takes for granted that what is true of musicians who play in nightclubs is true of musicians who play elsewhere
presumes, without providing justification, that the audiologists’ warnings were based on a sample that was too small
treats one person’s experience as sufficient to show that a claim about the risk to a whole population is exaggerated
takes for granted that the hearing test the uncle took last month gave an accurate measure of his hearing
questions.explanation: A claim about increased risk is a claim about how often hearing loss occurs across many people exposed to loud music, so one drummer with normal hearing is fully compatible with it; (D) names this. (E) is tempting, but it questions a premise rather than the reasoning: even a perfectly accurate test of one person could not show that the risk to everyone is exaggerated.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Audiologists have exaggerated the danger that loud music poses to hearing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The blogger’s uncle has drummed in loud clubs for forty years and his hearing tested normal for his age.

breakdown.analysis: So what if one drummer is fine? “Increased risk” never meant every exposed person goes deaf. It means hearing loss happens more often in the exposed group. One lucky case can’t tell you anything about how often something happens. It’s like arguing: my friend eats fast food every day and is healthy, so doctors exaggerate the risks of fast food. This is the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw, a classic; know it. We need an answer that says one case can’t refute a claim about risk across many people.

choices.note: So? The argument doesn’t need a threshold. Even with one, a single healthy drummer still wouldn’t show the risk is exaggerated.
The blogger never generalizes from nightclub musicians to other musicians. The jump is from one person to everyone exposed to loud music.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Jazz players in clubs rarely read sheet music, so orchestra players must rarely read it either.

choices.note: The blogger says nothing about how the audiologists reached their warning. Ironically, it’s the blogger who relies on a sample of one.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The study surely used too few people, so its findings can be dismissed.

choices.note: CORRECT. “Increased risk” is a claim about how often hearing loss shows up across many exposed people. One drummer with normal hearing fits perfectly well with that claim. A single case can’t show the risk is overstated.

Tempting, because it pokes at the evidence. But that’s a premise objection: an argument is entitled to rely on its stated facts, and LSAT flaw answers describe the gap between evidence and conclusion. Grant that the test was perfect, and one healthy drummer still can’t show that a population-wide risk is overstated.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The thermometer read 20 degrees, so it was 20 degrees, even though the thermometer had not been checked in years.

questions.stimulus: Last year the health department of Corrin ran a campaign urging residents over forty to have their blood pressure checked, and it offered free checks at local pharmacies. During the following year, the number of Corrin residents being treated for high blood pressure rose by a third, even though there is no evidence that residents’ diets, weight, or exercise habits changed during that period.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the rise in the number of Corrin residents being treated for high blood pressure?
choices: High blood pressure is considerably more common among people over forty than among younger people.
The campaign’s advertisements also urged residents to reduce the amount of salt in their diets.
Some of the residents who had their blood pressure checked as a result of the campaign learned that it was normal.
Many Corrin residents who already had high blood pressure before the campaign had not known that they had it.
In a neighboring city that ran no such campaign, the number of residents treated for high blood pressure stayed about the same.
questions.explanation: If many residents already had undiagnosed high blood pressure, the screening campaign would bring them into treatment without any change in the underlying condition, which is (D). (E) is tempting because it ties the rise to the campaign, but it only shows that the campaign made a difference; it doesn’t say how a checkup campaign could raise treatment numbers when health habits stayed the same.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Residents’ habits didn’t change, but after a screening campaign the number being treated for high blood pressure jumped by a third.

breakdown.analysis: How can more people be treated if nobody got less healthy? Easy: they were already sick and nobody knew. A campaign that gets people checked finds cases that were there all along. It’s like a new smoke detector “causing” more fire alarms: the smoke was already there, now somebody is noticing it. We need an answer that says there were hidden cases waiting to be found.

choices.note: So? This was true before and after the campaign. A constant fact can’t explain a change. It also doesn’t explain why the targeted group suddenly showed up for treatment.
This pushes the wrong way. Less salt would tend to lower blood pressure, so if anything it makes the rise more puzzling.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. People with normal readings wouldn’t be treated, so they don’t help explain more treatment.

CORRECT. If lots of residents had high blood pressure without knowing it, a campaign that gets them checked would diagnose them and put them into treatment. More treatment, same health habits. That’s the whole puzzle solved.

Tempting, because it points to the campaign as the cause. But the puzzle is how a checkup campaign could raise treatment numbers when nothing about health changed. This shows the campaign mattered; it doesn’t show how.

questions.stimulus:
Imre: Cities should be willing to name new streets after people who are still living. Honoring someone while that person can appreciate the honor makes the tribute more meaningful, and it encourages others to serve their communities.

Dana: A living person’s reputation is never settled. If someone honored with a street name is later disgraced, the city must either keep a name that embarrasses residents or go to the expense and confusion of renaming the street.
questions.stem: Imre and Dana disagree over whether
choices: cities should be willing to name new streets after people who are still living
honoring a person while that person is still alive makes a tribute to that person more meaningful
renaming a street causes expense and confusion for a city and its residents
the reputations of people who have died are more settled than those of people who are living
a city that has named a street after a living person should rename the street if that person is later disgraced
questions.explanation: Imre says cities should be willing to name streets after living people; Dana gives a reason against doing so, so they disagree about (A). (D) is tempting because Dana implies it, but Imre takes no position on reputations, and in (E) Dana describes renaming as one of two bad options without endorsing it, while Imre never raises it.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Imre: Name new streets after living people; the honor means more and encourages service.; Dana: A living person may later be disgraced, leaving the city with an embarrassing name or a costly renaming.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Imre’s yes is explicit: cities should be willing to do this. Dana never says “no” in so many words, but the whole reply is a reason against it, and that’s how LSAT dialogues usually work. Test each choice: does Imre have a view? Does Dana? Do the views clash? Only one choice survives all three questions.

choices.note: CORRECT. Imre says yes in the first sentence. Dana’s whole point is a reason not to: a living person might be disgraced, leaving the city with a bad name or a costly change. One says yes, the other says no.
Only Imre speaks to this. Dana never says whether a living honoree’s appreciation adds meaning; Dana worries about what happens later.
Only Dana says this. Imre never mentions renaming, so we don’t know Imre’s view. To disagree, both have to take a side.
Dana hints at this, but Imre says nothing about reputations at all. One-sided, so it can’t be the point of disagreement.

Tempting, because renaming is Dana’s topic. But Dana only lays out the two bad options, keeping an embarrassing name or paying to rename, without choosing one, and Imre never discusses disgrace or renaming. Neither speaker takes a side here.

questions.stimulus: Hotel manager: Guests who booked their stays through our own website rated those stays higher, on average, than guests who booked through travel agencies. Our website shows photos of every type of room we offer, whereas the agencies’ listings show only a single photo of our lobby. Therefore, if we persuade the agencies to show photos of all our room types, guests who book through them will rate their stays higher.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the hotel manager’s argument?
choices: Guests who book through the hotel’s own website are more likely than other guests to stay at the hotel again in the future.
At least some guests who book through travel agencies would look at the photos in an agency’s listing before arriving.
At least half of the guests who book through travel agencies choose a hotel mainly on the basis of the photos that its listing displays.
Guests rate a stay higher whenever the room they are given matches what they expected from photos seen before booking.
At least one of the travel agencies would agree to show photos of every room type if the hotel asked it to do so.
questions.explanation: The plan works only through the photos, so it requires that at least some agency bookers would actually see them; (B) is that minimal requirement. (C) is hedged too, but “at least half” choosing mainly by photos is more than the plan needs: if only a few agency bookers look at the photos, the plan can still raise their ratings. (E) is tempting, but the conclusion is conditional (“if we persuade the agencies”), so it does not depend on even one agency agreeing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the agencies show photos of all room types, agency bookers will rate their stays higher.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Website bookers rate stays higher; the website shows every room type, the agencies show only the lobby.

breakdown.analysis: What has to be true for photos on the agency listings to change anything? Somebody has to look at them. If not a single agency booker ever glances at the listing photos, adding more photos does nothing. That’s the minimal assumption. We need an answer that says at least some agency bookers would see the photos. Don’t pick an answer just because it starts “at least”: three choices here are hedged, and you still have to negate each one. And notice the conclusion is an if-then. The manager isn’t claiming the agencies will agree, only what happens if they do.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Repeat stays aren’t ratings. Negate it (website bookers are no more likely to return) and the argument is untouched.
choices.negation: Guests who book through the website are not more likely than other guests to stay again.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: no agency booker would look at the listing photos before arriving. Then new photos can’t shape anyone’s expectations or choices, and the plan can’t raise ratings. The argument collapses, so this is required.
choices.negation: No guests who book through travel agencies would look at the photos in an agency’s listing before arriving.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s hedged and it’s the same idea as (B), turned up. But “at least half” is still more than the argument needs. Negate it: fewer than half of agency bookers choose mainly by photos. Plenty could still look at the photos, and the ones who do could have better-matched stays. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Fewer than half of the guests who book through travel agencies choose a hotel mainly on the basis of its listing photos.

choices.note: Tempting, because it spells out a way the plan could work. But “whenever” makes it a strong rule the manager doesn’t need. Negate it: matching expectations doesn’t always raise ratings. Photos could still help most of the time, or help in another way (guests picking rooms they like). The argument survives.
choices.negation: Guests do not always rate a stay higher when the room matches what they expected from the photos.

choices.note: Tempting, because the hedge makes it look minimal and the plan seems to need it. But the conclusion is conditional: “if we persuade the agencies.” The manager predicts what happens if they agree, not that any will. Negate it and the if-then still stands.
choices.negation: None of the travel agencies would agree to show photos of every room type, even if the hotel asked.

questions.stimulus: For its spring exhibit, the Lindqvist Gallery used wall labels that gave only each work’s title and date, and many visitors complained that the labels were uninformative. Yet visitors to that exhibit spent more time, on average, in front of each work than visitors to any of the gallery’s previous exhibits, and a larger share of them bought the exhibit catalog.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many of the complaints about the labels came from visitors who had also attended several of the gallery’s previous exhibits.
The catalog for the spring exhibit was priced lower than the catalogs that the gallery had produced for its previous exhibits.
People given little written context for a work of art tend to study the work itself longer and to seek that context from other sources.
Visitors who complain about an exhibit are less likely than other visitors to return to the gallery for its later exhibits.
The spring exhibit contained fewer works than any of the gallery’s previous exhibits, though visitors stayed about as long in the gallery overall.
questions.explanation: Sparse labels left visitors without background, which explains the complaints; if people who lack written context look harder at the work and look elsewhere for the context, the longer viewing and the catalog sales follow too. (C) covers all three facts. (E) is the trap: fewer works with the same total visit time explains the extra time per work, but not why more visitors bought the catalog.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Visitors complained that the labels were uninformative, but they spent more time per work and bought the catalog more often than at any earlier exhibit.

breakdown.analysis: How can bad labels go with more engagement? Maybe the bad labels caused it. If you’re told almost nothing about a painting, you have to actually look at it, and if you want the backstory you have to get it somewhere else, like the catalog. We need an answer that turns the thin labels into a reason for both the longer looking and the catalog sales. Watch for answers that explain only one of the two.

choices.note: So? Who complained doesn’t explain why visitors lingered longer or bought more catalogs. Repeat visitors noticing the change explains the complaints, which needed no explaining.
Tempting, because a cheaper catalog would sell better. But it explains only the catalog sales. Why did people spend more time in front of each work? This answer is silent.

CORRECT. Little written context → people study the art itself longer (more time per work) and look for the missing context elsewhere (the catalog). The very thing visitors complained about produces both surprising results.
Irrelevant. Whether complainers come back later says nothing about how this exhibit’s visitors behaved while they were there.

Tempting, and the best trap here. Fewer works and the same total visit means more time per work, so half the puzzle goes away. But the catalog sales are left unexplained. A good resolution covers every surprising fact.

questions.stimulus: Every person registered for the Halloway Design Conference either collects a name badge at the front desk on the opening morning or has had a badge mailed in advance. A badge is mailed only to a registrant who requested mailing at least two weeks before the conference. Every registrant who collects a badge at the front desk is photographed for the conference directory. Owen Strand registered for the conference, but he was not photographed for the directory.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any registrant who requested mailing at least two weeks before the conference had a badge mailed in advance.
Owen Strand collected a badge at the front desk but declined to be photographed for the directory.
Some registrants who had badges mailed in advance were also photographed for the conference directory.
Owen Strand requested at least two weeks before the conference that his badge be mailed.
Owen Strand registered for the conference less than two weeks before the conference began.
questions.explanation: Owen wasn’t photographed, so he didn’t collect a badge at the desk; a registrant who didn’t collect at the desk had a badge mailed; and mailing requires a request at least two weeks ahead, so (D) must be true. (A) reverses the second rule: a timely request is required for mailing, not a guarantee of it.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Registered → collects at desk OR badge mailed; 2. mailed → requested at least two weeks ahead; 3. collects at desk → photographed; 4. Owen registered and was not photographed.

breakdown.analysis: Start with Owen and chain the rules. Not photographed → (contrapositive of 3) didn’t collect at the desk. Registered and not at the desk → (rule 1) badge mailed. Mailed → (rule 2) requested at least two weeks ahead. Chain: not photographed → not desk → mailed → timely request. Watch for the answer that runs rule 2 backwards: “only to those who requested” makes the request necessary, not sufficient.

choices.note: This reverses the second rule. A timely request is required for mailing (“only to”), not a guarantee of it. Necessary isn’t sufficient.
Can’t be true. Everyone who collects at the desk is photographed, and Owen wasn’t. So he didn’t collect at the desk.
Could be true, but nothing requires it. The rules say desk collectors are photographed; they say nothing about whether anyone with a mailed badge was.
CORRECT. Not photographed → didn’t collect at the desk. Registered and didn’t collect at the desk → badge was mailed. Mailed → requested at least two weeks ahead. So Owen made a timely request.

Backwards, if anything. The chain shows Owen requested mailing at least two weeks ahead, and only registrants get badges mailed, so he was very likely registered well before the conference. Nothing forces this; it’s there for people who misread “two weeks.”

questions.stimulus: Drivers in a city’s older neighborhoods, where streets are narrow and lined with parked cars, have fewer collisions per mile driven than do drivers in the city’s newer neighborhoods, where streets are wide. Traffic engineers attribute the difference to the narrow streets themselves: drivers who feel hemmed in tend to drive more slowly and more cautiously.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the traffic engineers’ argument?
choices: Drivers in the city’s older neighborhoods are, on average, older and more experienced than drivers in its newer neighborhoods.
Speed measurements show that drivers who regularly use both narrow and wide streets in the city drive markedly slower on the narrow ones.
Collisions in the newer neighborhoods are more likely to result in serious injuries than are collisions that occur in the older neighborhoods.
Cars parked along narrow streets sometimes block drivers’ view of pedestrians who are about to step into the street.
Several cities have recently narrowed some of their wide streets in an effort to reduce the number of collisions occurring on them.
questions.explanation: The engineers’ story has a mechanism: narrow streets make drivers slow down. (B) confirms that mechanism, and it does so with the same drivers on both kinds of street, so the slowing can’t be credited to who lives in the older neighborhoods. (A) points to the drivers instead, which weakens, and (C) shifts from how many collisions there are to how serious they are.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The narrow streets themselves cause the older neighborhoods’ lower collision rate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Older neighborhoods have narrow streets and fewer collisions per mile than newer neighborhoods with wide streets; hemmed-in drivers slow down.

breakdown.analysis: Is it the streets, or the people driving on them? The engineers don’t just point to a correlation; they name a mechanism: hemmed-in drivers slow down and take more care. One good way to strengthen a causal claim is to show the proposed mechanism actually operates. Even better if it operates in a way that rules out the obvious rival cause, different drivers. We need an answer that shows narrow streets really do change how people drive.

choices.note: Opposite. Older, more experienced drivers are a rival explanation for the lower collision rate. That weakens the claim that the streets are responsible.

CORRECT. The engineers say narrow streets make drivers slow down. Here the very same drivers slow down when the street narrows. That confirms the mechanism, and because the drivers are held constant, the effect can’t be chalked up to who lives in the older neighborhoods.
Tempting, because it sounds like more evidence that the old neighborhoods are safer. But the argument is about how often collisions happen, not how bad they are. Different measure.
If anything, this cuts the other way: it describes a danger narrow streets create. It doesn’t help show they reduce collisions or make drivers more careful.
So? Other cities trying it shows what officials believe, not that it works. A popular plan isn’t evidence for the causal claim.

questions.stimulus: Under the rules of the Morvan appellate court, any appeal that raises a constitutional question must be heard by the full court rather than by a three-judge panel. Moreover, the state attorney general is entitled to intervene in every appeal that challenges the validity of a statute. The Tessaly appeal has been assigned to a three-judge panel. Hence, the attorney general is not entitled to intervene in the Tessaly appeal.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every appeal that challenges the validity of a statute raises a constitutional question.
The attorney general is entitled to intervene only in appeals that raise a constitutional question.
In every appeal that raises a constitutional question, the attorney general is entitled to intervene.
Any appeal that is heard by the full court raises a constitutional question.
The attorney general seldom intervenes in appeals that are heard by a three-judge panel.
questions.explanation: Panel → no constitutional question (contrapositive of the first rule). The conclusion is about the attorney general’s entitlement, so the bridge must run from entitlement to a constitutional question; (B) supplies it: entitled → constitutional question → full court, so a panel appeal carries no entitlement. (A) is the trap: it shows the Tessaly appeal challenges no statute, but the statute rule gives only one way the attorney general can be entitled, not the only way.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The attorney general is not entitled to intervene in the Tessaly appeal.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Constitutional question → full court; challenges a statute → attorney general entitled; Tessaly is before a three-judge panel.

breakdown.analysis: Chain what you have. Tessaly is before a panel, so (contrapositive of rule 1) it raises no constitutional question. Now look at the conclusion: no entitlement to intervene. The statute rule is a trap: statute → entitled tells you one way to get entitlement, and knowing Tessaly isn’t a statute case can’t rule out other ways. We need a rule that makes entitlement impossible without a constitutional question: entitled → constitutional question. Then: panel → no constitutional question → not entitled. Most students pick (A) because it links the two premises neatly. It fails because it only proves Tessaly isn’t a statute challenge, and that’s denying the sufficient condition of rule 2.

choices.note: Tempting, and it’s the trap. With it, Tessaly raises no constitutional question, so it challenges no statute. But rule 2 says a statute challenge is enough for entitlement, not that it’s required. The attorney general could be entitled for some other reason. Conclusion still open.
CORRECT. Entitled → constitutional question → full court. Contrapositive: panel → no constitutional question → not entitled. Tessaly is before a panel, so the conclusion follows.
This reverses the link we need. Constitutional question → entitled tells you about appeals that do raise one. Tessaly doesn’t, so this says nothing about it.
This reverses rule 1 and never mentions the attorney general. Even with it, nothing connects the panel to entitlement.
“Seldom” is about what the attorney general does, not what the attorney general is entitled to do, and it leaves room for exceptions. Not sufficient.

questions.stimulus: Researchers played two groups of volunteers the same recording of a short piano piece. One group was told that the performer was a renowned concert pianist; the other was told that the performer was a first-year conservatory student. The first group rated the performance as far more technically accomplished than the second group did, yet the two groups reported enjoying the piece equally.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: How much listeners enjoy a performance is unaffected by what they believe about who is performing it.
Renowned concert pianists generally play with greater technical skill than do students in their first year at a conservatory.
Volunteers who were told that the performer was a student would have enjoyed the piece more had they been told nothing about the performer.
A belief about a performer can sway some of a listener’s judgments about a performance while leaving others unaffected.
Listeners judge a performance’s technical accomplishment chiefly by what they have been told about the performer rather than by what they hear.
questions.explanation: Both groups heard the identical recording, so the difference in technical ratings must come from what they were told; yet their enjoyment did not differ. Together these support the modest claim in (D): a belief about the performer moved one judgment and not another. (A) generalizes the single enjoyment result into a universal law, and (E) inflates “affected” into “chiefly determined.”

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Both groups heard the same recording; 2. one was told “famous pianist,” the other “first-year student”; 3. the first group rated it far more technically accomplished; 4. both groups enjoyed it equally.

breakdown.analysis: Same sound, different labels, different skill ratings: the label did that. But the enjoyment scores didn’t move. Put the two together: the label changed one judgment and left another alone. Hard to prephrase beyond that, so watch for answers that take one result and blow it up into a rule about all listeners, or that turn “affected” into “mostly determined.”

choices.note: Tempting, because it reuses the enjoyment result. But one study in which two groups averaged the same enjoyment can’t show that enjoyment is never affected by beliefs about performers, for anyone, anywhere. Too strong.
Irrelevant. Both groups heard the same recording. The study tells us nothing about how real concert pianists play compared with students.
We don’t know this. There was no group that was told nothing, so the study gives no baseline for what “told nothing” would have produced.
CORRECT. Technical ratings moved with the label; enjoyment didn’t. That’s exactly “some judgments swayed, others left alone.” Modest, and it combines both halves of the result.
Tempting, because the label clearly mattered. But “chiefly” is a ranking the study can’t support. The label could have nudged ratings while the sound itself still did most of the work.

questions.stimulus: Coach: Lena missed three of the team’s last five practices to care for her sick grandmother, and our rules say that any player who misses more than two practices in a month must sit out the next game. Even so, Lena should play on Saturday. The rule exists to ensure that players are prepared and committed, and Lena kept up with the drills on her own and has shown her commitment all season.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the coach’s reasoning?
choices: A rule should not be enforced against someone in a case in which enforcing it would serve none of the purposes the rule was adopted to achieve.
A player who misses practice for a good reason should be excused from a team rule only if the player told the coach about the absences in advance.
A coach should weigh a player’s commitment over an entire season, and not just recent attendance, in deciding how much that player plays.
Team rules should be enforced in the same way for every player, since exceptions weaken players’ confidence that they are treated fairly.
A player who misses practice to care for a family member has shown a kind of commitment that a team ought to value.
questions.explanation: The coach grants that Lena broke the rule but argues that its purposes, preparation and commitment, are already met in her case. (A) turns that into a rule: when enforcement would serve none of a rule’s purposes, don’t enforce it. (B) states only a necessary condition for an excuse, so it can’t establish that Lena should play, and (C) tells the coach to consider commitment without saying the attendance rule may be set aside.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lena should play on Saturday despite breaking the attendance rule.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The rule exists to ensure preparation and commitment; Lena kept up with drills on her own and has shown commitment all season.

breakdown.analysis: The coach admits the rule applies. So why ignore it? Because the rule’s reasons don’t reach Lena: it’s there to make sure players are ready and committed, and she is both. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. Here: if enforcing a rule wouldn’t serve its purpose, don’t enforce it. Watch for answers that sound sympathetic to Lena but never get you to “she plays.”

choices.note: CORRECT. Sufficient condition: enforcing the rule would serve none of its purposes. The coach supplies that (Lena is prepared and committed). Verdict: don’t enforce it, so she plays. Facts in, conclusion out.

Tempting, because it mentions a good reason for missing practice. But “only if” gives a requirement for an excuse, not a guarantee. And we don’t know whether Lena told the coach in advance. It can’t get you to “Lena plays.”

Tempting, because it talks about season-long commitment. But weighing commitment in deciding playing time doesn’t say the attendance rule can be set aside. Under this principle the rule could still bench her.
Opposite. This would bench Lena, not play her.
Nice sentiment, but it stops short. Valuing her commitment doesn’t tell you that a rule she broke shouldn’t be applied. No verdict about Saturday.

questions.stimulus: A month-long study asked forty office workers to keep their phones outside the bedroom every night. By the end of the month, the workers reported falling asleep faster, on average, than they had during the month before the study began. The researchers concluded that keeping one’s phone out of the bedroom helps people fall asleep faster.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers’ argument?
choices: Comparable workers who kept their phones in the bedroom that month fell asleep no faster than before.
Most of the forty workers said at the outset that they expected the change to help them fall asleep faster.
Several of the workers in the study also reported waking up less often during the night than they had before.
Retired people in the same city who kept their phones in the bedroom that month fell asleep no faster than before.
The month of the study was one in which the hours of daylight were growing noticeably shorter.
questions.explanation: The before-and-after comparison leaves open that something else about that month made people fall asleep faster; (A) shows comparable workers who kept their phones nearby in the same month saw no change, which rules that out. (D) is the near-miss: it offers a control group, but retirees differ from office workers in exactly the ways a month-specific cause (such as work stress) would matter. (B) and (E) suggest alternative causes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Keeping one’s phone out of the bedroom helps people fall asleep faster.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Workers who kept phones out of the bedroom for a month fell asleep faster than they had the month before.

breakdown.analysis: What if everyone fell asleep faster that month: cooler nights, less work stress, the novelty of being in a study? Then the phone had nothing to do with it. A before-and-after study with no comparison group can’t separate the phone from everything else that changed. We need an answer that shows people who did NOT move their phones didn’t improve.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same kind of workers, same month, phones still in the bedroom: no change. That rules out the idea that something about the month made everyone fall asleep faster, so the phone change looks like the cause.
Opposite. If the workers expected to fall asleep faster, expectation alone could explain the self-reported improvement. That’s a rival cause, so it weakens.
Tempting, because it sounds like more good news. But the conclusion is about falling asleep faster, not waking less. A different benefit doesn’t support this claim.

Tempting, and it’s the trap: it looks like the control group you were hunting for. But retirees aren’t comparable to office workers: no commute, no workday stress, different schedules. Something about that month (say, a lighter workload) could have helped the office workers and not touched retirees. (A) uses comparable workers, so it does the job far better.
This hints at a different explanation, since changing daylight can affect sleep. If anything, it weakens.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Some critics hold that a translation is faithful only to the extent that it uses the word in the new language that most closely matches each word of the original. By that standard, rendering the French idiom “il pleut des cordes” word for word as “it is raining ropes” would be more faithful than rendering it “it is pouring.” That is plainly wrong, since readers of the literal version would not grasp what the original says. So the critics’ standard should be rejected.
questions.stem: The claim that a word-for-word rendering of the idiom would be more faithful plays which one of the following roles in the editor’s argument?
choices: It is the overall conclusion that the editor’s argument as a whole is designed to establish.
It is a consequence of the critics’ standard that the editor uses to show the standard is mistaken.
It is an example offered to show that some idioms cannot be faithfully translated at all.
It is a premise that the critics themselves offer in support of their standard of faithful translation.
It is a claim that the editor accepts but argues is irrelevant to evaluating the critics’ standard.
questions.explanation: The editor derives the claim from the critics’ standard (“by that standard”) and then calls it “plainly wrong,” so the claim is an absurd consequence used to sink the standard, which is (B). (D) is tempting, but the critics never offer this claim; the editor draws it out of their view in order to reject it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics’ word-matching standard of faithfulness should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: By that standard, “it is raining ropes” would count as more faithful than “it is pouring”; that result is plainly wrong, because readers wouldn’t grasp the original’s meaning.

breakdown.analysis: Does the editor believe the word-for-word version is more faithful? No: the editor calls that “plainly wrong.” The editor doesn’t believe this. It’s the absurd result the editor derives from the critics’ rule in order to sink it. It’s like answering “never tell a lie” by pointing out it would require telling a burglar where your kids are hiding.

choices.note: The conclusion is that the standard should be rejected, flagged by “So.” The editor doesn’t even believe the word-for-word claim, so it can’t be what the argument sets out to prove.
CORRECT. “By that standard” marks it as following from the critics’ view, and “that is plainly wrong” marks the editor rejecting it. A consequence used to show the standard is mistaken.
The editor shows the idiom can be translated perfectly well, as “it is pouring.” The point is about which translation is more faithful, not about untranslatable idioms.

Tempting, because the claim comes from the critics’ standard. But the critics never offer it as a reason. The editor derives it from their view in order to attack it. A premise of theirs would support their standard, not embarrass it.
The editor doesn’t accept the claim; it calls it plainly wrong. And far from being irrelevant, it’s the editor’s main weapon against the standard.

questions.stimulus: The unusually long antennae of male Calopha virens leaf beetles, nearly twice the length of the females’, most likely serve mainly to help the males find mates. In many insect species, males locate mates by detecting airborne chemicals released by females, and longer antennae can hold more of the sensory cells that detect such chemicals.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, weakens the argument EXCEPT:
choices: In related species of leaf beetle in which the males have short antennae, the males locate females mainly by sight.
Male C. virens use their antennae chiefly to fence with rival males over the best feeding sites.
Female C. virens do not release any airborne chemicals that the males of their species are able to detect.
In male C. virens, the cells that detect airborne chemicals are confined to the third of each antenna nearest the head.
Male C. virens whose antennae have been trimmed to the length of the females’ find mates as quickly as males with intact antennae.
questions.explanation: The argument infers a mate-finding function from length plus an analogy to other insects. (B) offers a rival function, (C) removes the chemicals the antennae would detect, (D) shows the extra length adds no detecting cells, and (E) shows the extra length doesn’t help in finding mates. (A) concerns other species with short antennae; if anything it fits the idea that long antennae signal a scent-based search, so it does not weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The long antennae of male C. virens probably serve mainly to help them find mates.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Males’ antennae are twice as long as females’; in many insects males find mates by detecting females’ airborne chemicals, and longer antennae can hold more detecting cells.

breakdown.analysis: The argument is a function guess: the trait is “probably for X.” It can be hurt in several ways: show the trait does something else, show the chemicals aren’t there to detect, show the extra length doesn’t add detectors, or show the length doesn’t help in finding mates. Four answers do one of these. In an EXCEPT question, the right answer is the one that doesn’t weaken; it can strengthen or do nothing. Check each choice against this species and this trait.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is about other species, and short-antennaed ones at that. Males without long antennae relying on sight is, if anything, what you’d expect if long antennae are for a scent search. It doesn’t give a reason to doubt the argument. Tempting to call it a weakener (“beetles can find mates by sight”), but it says nothing about C. virens.
Weakens. A rival function: if the antennae are mainly fencing weapons, they don’t serve mainly to find mates.
Weakens. If females give off no chemicals the males can detect, the antennae can’t be finding mates by smell. The analogy to other insects breaks down.
Weakens. The argument needs longer antennae to hold more detecting cells. If the cells sit only near the head, the extra length adds none.
Weakens. A direct test: cut the antennae to female length and the males find mates just as fast. So the extra length isn’t helping them find mates.

questions.stimulus: Intense activity during deep sleep in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory, helps people retain what they learned before sleeping. In a recent study, volunteers studied a list of words before going to bed and were later woken during deep sleep and asked to recall the list. Brain scans taken just before waking showed intense hippocampal activity in nearly every volunteer who recalled the list well.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that all of the volunteers studied the list of words with roughly equal care and effort
fails to consider that being woken during deep sleep may make it harder to recall what one has learned
fails to rule out the possibility that recalling the list well caused the intense activity in the hippocampus
overlooks the possibility that such activity is typical of deep sleep in nearly everyone, however good their recall
draws a conclusion about people in general from a study of volunteers who may not be representative of most people
questions.explanation: The scans are reported only for volunteers who recalled the list well; if nearly everyone shows intense hippocampal activity in deep sleep, poor recallers included, the activity can’t be what helps retention, and (D) describes that missing comparison without naming the group. (C) is the trap: reverse causation is the textbook causal flaw, but the scans were taken before anyone was woken and asked to recall, so the recall can’t have caused the activity.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Intense hippocampal activity during deep sleep helps people retain what they learned before sleeping.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly every volunteer who recalled the list well showed intense hippocampal activity just before being woken.

breakdown.analysis: So nearly every good recaller had intense hippocampal activity. What about the poor recallers? If their brains lit up the same way, the activity is just what deep sleep looks like, and it has nothing to do with remembering. The argument checks only one group. It’s like noting that nearly every lottery winner drank coffee that morning without asking how many losers did. We need an answer that raises the missing comparison. (D) does, but in disguise: it never mentions poor recallers, it just says the activity might be typical of nearly everyone. Most students pick (C) because reverse causation is the first causal flaw they hunt for, and (C) reuses the stimulus’s own words. It fails on timing: the scans were taken just before waking, and the recall came afterward, so recalling can’t have produced the activity.

choices.note: Merely possible. Uneven effort might add noise, but it doesn’t explain why good recall goes with intense activity, and the argument never relies on equal effort.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Students who used the new textbook scored higher, so the textbook works (ignoring that some students simply studied harder).

choices.note: So? If being woken hurts recall, it hurts everyone’s recall. That doesn’t explain why the good recallers had intense activity.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new test format lowered scores, so students learned less this year (ignoring that the harder format affected everyone).

choices.note: Tempting. Reverse causation is the classic causal flaw, and this answer borrows the stimulus’s wording. But check the timing: the scans were taken just before the volunteers were woken, and they recalled the list only afterward. A later event can’t cause an earlier one, so the argument doesn’t commit this flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: People who own running shoes run more, so owning running shoes makes people run (when running is why they bought the shoes).

choices.note: CORRECT. If intense hippocampal activity shows up in deep sleep for nearly everyone, poor recallers included, it can’t be what separates good retention from bad. That’s the missing-comparison-group flaw, stated without naming the missing group.
A generic study complaint. Nothing suggests these volunteers are unusual, and a perfectly representative sample would still leave the real problem: no data on poor recallers.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Members of our running club love the new shoes, so most people will love them.

questions.stimulus: Judge: During the trial, juror Pell admitted that he had searched online for the defendant’s name, though he says he found nothing about the case. Even if Pell is telling the truth, he should be removed from the jury. It is essential that the public be able to see that a verdict rests only on the evidence presented in court.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the judge’s reasoning?
choices: A juror who searches online for information about a case should be removed from the jury if the search turned up anything about that case.
Jurors who are candid with the court about their own misconduct should be treated more leniently than jurors who try to conceal it.
If a juror’s conduct could lead the public to doubt that a verdict rests only on courtroom evidence, the court should determine what the juror actually learned.
Anyone whose conduct gives others reason to suspect that a decision was improperly influenced should be excluded from making it, whether or not it was.
Any juror who has misled the court about his or her conduct during a trial should be removed from the jury.
questions.explanation: The judge would remove Pell even if his search found nothing, because what matters is whether the public can see the verdict as untainted. (D) says that conduct giving others grounds for suspicion is enough for exclusion, whether or not any actual influence occurred. (A) borrows the stimulus’s words but makes removal depend on finding something, which the judge explicitly sets aside, and (C) has the right trigger but the wrong remedy: it calls for an inquiry into what Pell learned, which the judge treats as beside the point.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pell should be removed from the jury, even if he found nothing about the case.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pell searched online for the defendant’s name; the public must be able to see that a verdict rests only on courtroom evidence.

breakdown.analysis: Why remove a juror who may have learned nothing? Because the issue isn’t what he learned; it’s how it looks. “Even if Pell is telling the truth” tells you actual contamination is beside the point. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. We need: conduct that could make people suspect the verdict is tainted → remove the person, whether or not it was really tainted. The right answer may not say “juror” at all; it can be a general rule about anyone in a decision.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses the stimulus’s own words: searched online, removed. But it makes removal depend on the search turning something up, and the judge says Pell should go even if it turned up nothing. Wrong condition.
If anything, this cuts toward keeping Pell, who admitted the search. It doesn’t get you to removal.

Tempting, because it has exactly the right trigger: conduct that could make the public doubt the verdict. But the verdict is wrong. It calls for finding out what Pell learned, and the judge says Pell goes even if he learned nothing. Right condition, wrong remedy.

CORRECT. Pell’s search gives the public reason to suspect the verdict could be influenced, and “whether or not it was” covers the case where he found nothing. Conduct → reason for suspicion → exclusion. That’s the judge’s reasoning in general form.
Doesn’t apply. Nothing says Pell misled the court; the judge assumes he may be telling the truth. A rule about liars can’t justify removing him.

questions.stimulus: Of the thousands of surviving letters that soldiers sent home during a long nineteenth-century war, fewer than one in fifty criticizes the war. Some scholars take this as evidence that the soldiers overwhelmingly supported it. But the scarcity of critical letters more likely reflects the soldiers’ caution than their actual views: army censors read the soldiers’ outgoing mail, and the soldiers knew it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Some soldiers worked out private codes with their families so that complaints about the war could pass the censors unnoticed.
Soldiers’ diaries from the war, which the censors never saw, express approval of the war about as often as the soldiers’ letters do.
Many soldiers’ diaries from the war mention that letters home were read by army censors before they were sent.
The soldiers’ letters that newspapers printed during the war were selected by editors who generally supported the war.
Soldiers who were known to have criticized the war in their letters home were seldom punished for having done so.
questions.explanation: The argument says caution about censors, not support, explains the shortage of critical letters. (A) shows soldiers who held critical views and disguised them precisely to get past the censors, so some letters that look uncritical concealed criticism. (C) only confirms that soldiers knew of the censors, a premise already granted, and (B) and (E) weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The scarcity of critical letters more likely reflects soldiers’ caution than their actual views.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fewer than one in fifty surviving letters criticizes the war; censors read soldiers’ mail, and soldiers knew it.

breakdown.analysis: Two explanations compete: soldiers really liked the war, or they kept quiet because the censors were reading. How would you tell them apart? Look for evidence that soldiers had criticism and hid it from the censors. Watch for answers that just repeat that the censors existed: the argument already grants that. And watch for answers about uncensored writing: check which way they point.

choices.note: CORRECT. Hard to like, because it says only “some” and never mentions the letter count. But look at what it shows: soldiers who had complaints about the war, and who hid them because of the censors. Those disguised complaints would be counted as non-critical letters. That’s the caution the argument says explains the scarcity.
Tempting, because it mentions writing the censors never saw. But read the direction: uncensored diaries are as approving as the letters. That suggests the letters reflect real views. It weakens.

Tempting, and it’s the trap. It sounds like support for the censorship story. But the argument already says the soldiers knew their mail was read. Confirming a premise the argument has already granted adds nothing to the step from caution to conclusion.
Off target. Letters picked by pro-war editors are a different set from the surviving letters the scholars counted. A biased newspaper sample says nothing about the archive.
Opposite. If critics went unpunished, soldiers had less reason to be cautious, which makes the caution explanation weaker.

questions.stimulus: Every pottery studio in the Eastgate district that sells its work to restaurants fires its pieces in a gas kiln. The Wren Street studio, which is in the Eastgate district, fires its pieces in a gas kiln. So the Wren Street studio must be one of the district’s studios that sell their work to restaurants.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Only members of the Linden choir have been given keys to the rehearsal hall that the choir uses on weekday evenings. Tomas has been given a key to that rehearsal hall. So Tomas must be a member of the Linden choir.

Every restaurant on Mill Street that offers outdoor seating also serves breakfast on weekends. The Blue Heron, a restaurant on Mill Street, does not serve breakfast on weekends. So the Blue Heron must not offer outdoor seating.
Every violin made in the Pazzi workshop during the last century has a maple back. This violin was not made in the Pazzi workshop during the last century. So this violin must not have a maple back.

To be eligible for this year’s Granger Prize, a novel must have been published within the past two years. Mira Ravel’s novel came out last year. So Mira Ravel’s novel must be eligible for this year’s Granger Prize.

Most of the paintings in the Ostler collection that were acquired before 1950 are landscapes. This painting is in the Ostler collection and was acquired before 1950. So this painting must be a landscape.
questions.explanation: The argument reasons: sells to restaurants → gas kiln; Wren Street uses a gas kiln; so it sells to restaurants, treating a necessary condition as sufficient. (D) does the same once its “must” wording is translated: eligible → published recently; this novel was published recently; so it’s eligible. (A) looks like the same shape but is valid (key → member), and (C) is flawed in a different way, by negating the sufficient condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Wren Street studio must sell its work to restaurants.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every Eastgate studio that sells to restaurants uses a gas kiln; Wren Street uses a gas kiln.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; this one has B; so it has A (affirming the necessary condition).

breakdown.analysis: Is the kiln argument good? No. Lots of studios could use gas kilns without selling to restaurants. Sells to restaurants → gas kiln. Having the gas kiln doesn’t take you back to restaurants. It’s like saying every NBA player is tall, my cousin is tall, so he’s in the NBA. Now map each choice. Watch the wording: “must have been” and “only” both mark necessary conditions, so translate before you compare. The match has to be flawed in the same way, not just flawed. Most students pick (A) because it has the same surface shape as the kiln argument. It fails because “only” marks the key as enough to prove membership, so (A) is valid. The match, (D), hides behind “must have been,” which marks a necessary condition.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like the same shape: a group, a feature, and someone with the feature. But “only members have keys” means key → member. Tomas has a key, so he’s a member. That’s valid, and a valid argument can’t match a flawed one.
Outdoor seating → weekend breakfast; no weekend breakfast; so no outdoor seating. That’s the contrapositive, and it’s valid. A valid argument can’t match a flawed one.
Tempting, because it’s flawed and uses “every.” But it’s a different flaw: it negates the sufficient condition (not Pazzi, so not maple) instead of affirming the necessary one.

CORRECT. Translate “to be eligible, a novel must have been published recently”: eligible → published recently. Ravel’s novel came out recently, so it’s eligible. That treats the necessary condition as enough, exactly like the kiln argument.
Flawed, but differently: it treats “most” as “all.” The original’s premise is a true “every” statement; its error is running it backward.

questions.stimulus: Last year the town of Wexley began requiring shops on its main street to close by 9 p.m. Over the following twelve months, three of the street’s late-night businesses closed permanently, although none of its late-night businesses had closed in the five years before the rule took effect. The new rule, then, is what drove those three businesses out of business.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: The three late-night businesses were the only businesses on Wexley’s main street to close permanently last year.
None of the three businesses was struggling financially before the town began requiring shops to close by 9 p.m.
At least one of the three businesses that closed had earned most of its revenue after 9 p.m. before the rule took effect.
At least some of Wexley’s other late-night businesses lost a smaller share of their revenue under the new rule than the three that closed did.
At least one of the three businesses would have remained open through that year had the closing rule never been adopted.
questions.explanation: To say the rule drove the three businesses out, the argument must assume they would not all have closed anyway; (E) states the weakest form of that, and its negation (all three would have closed regardless) destroys the conclusion. (B) is the trap: a business can be struggling and still be pushed under by the rule, so its negation leaves the argument standing. (C) is hedged but still unneeded: a business could be ruined by losing well under half its revenue. (D) is hedged too, but the argument never compares the three with the survivors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The 9 p.m. closing rule drove the three businesses out of business.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the rule, three late-night businesses closed; none had closed in the five years before.

breakdown.analysis: What if those three were going under anyway? Then the rule didn’t drive them out; it just happened at the same time. That’s a counterfactual cause: to blame the rule, you have to assume the closures wouldn’t have happened without it. The required version is minimal: not all three would have closed regardless. Most students pick (B) because “they weren’t already struggling” sounds like exactly that defense. It fails because it’s too strong: a struggling business can still be the one the rule finishes off. Three answers here are hedged with “at least,” so the hedge alone won’t find the key. Negate each one and see which negation actually sinks the argument.

choices.note: So? Other closures on the street don’t matter. Negate it (some other shop also closed) and the rule could still have driven these three out.
choices.negation: Some other business on the main street also closed permanently last year.

choices.note: Tempting, and it’s the trap. It sounds like the needed defense. But it’s too strong. Negate it: at least one was struggling. A struggling business can still be pushed under by losing its late hours, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: At least one of the three businesses was struggling financially before the rule.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s hedged and it explains how the rule could hurt them. But the argument doesn’t need even one of them to have earned most of its revenue late. Negate it: each earned half or less after 9 p.m. Losing 30 or 40 percent of revenue can still sink a business. The argument survives.
choices.negation: None of the three businesses had earned most of its revenue after 9 p.m. before the rule took effect.

choices.note: Hedged, but a comparison the argument never relies on. Negate it: every other late-night business lost as large a share or larger. They may simply have had more cushion. The rule could still have driven the three out.
choices.negation: None of the other late-night businesses lost a smaller share of revenue under the rule than the three that closed did.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: all three would have closed that year even without the rule. Then the rule didn’t drive them out, and the conclusion collapses. Hedged, awkward, and required.
choices.negation: All three businesses would have closed that year even if the closing rule had never been adopted.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Councilor Brandt’s argument against the city’s subsidy for the municipal golf course cannot be accepted as it stands. Brandt argues that the subsidy should end because fewer than one resident in twenty uses the course in a typical year. Yet fewer than one resident in twenty uses the city’s public boat launch in a typical year, and Brandt has repeatedly voted to expand the launch.
questions.stem: The columnist’s argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that the boat launch and the golf course should be funded at similar levels because similar numbers of residents use them
rejecting Councilor Brandt’s argument on the grounds that Brandt, having voted to expand the launch, cannot judge public facilities impartially
challenging a criterion by showing that the person invoking it rejects a result the criterion would yield in another case
questioning the accuracy of the usage figures on which Councilor Brandt bases the argument against the golf course subsidy
concluding that the golf course subsidy should be continued because the case against it has not been established
questions.explanation: The columnist notes that Brandt’s low-use criterion would also count against the boat launch, which Brandt supports, and concludes only that Brandt’s argument cannot be accepted as it stands. (C) describes that move abstractly. (A) and (E) overstate the columnist’s conclusion: the columnist never says the two facilities deserve equal funding or that the subsidy should continue. (B) turns an inconsistency into an attack on Brandt’s character.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brandt’s argument against the golf course subsidy can’t be accepted as it stands.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brandt cites low use (under one in twenty residents); the boat launch has equally low use, and Brandt votes to expand it.

breakdown.analysis: What’s the columnist doing? Taking Brandt’s own test, “too few people use it,” and running it on something Brandt likes. If the test is good, it sinks the boat launch too, and Brandt clearly doesn’t accept that. So the test needs work. Notice how little the columnist concludes: not that the golf course deserves money, just that Brandt’s argument doesn’t work yet. Most students who miss this pick an answer that describes the comparison correctly but pins on a bigger conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because the comparison is right there. But the columnist never argues for equal funding; the conclusion is only that Brandt’s argument fails as it stands. Overstated conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this method: The library and the pool serve the same number of people, so they should get the same budget.

choices.note: Tempting, because it mentions Brandt’s vote. But the columnist uses the vote to show the criterion proves too much, not to say Brandt is biased or can’t be trusted.
choices.example: Example of this method: The councilor owns a boat, so his views on the launch should be ignored.

choices.note: CORRECT. The criterion is low use. Its proponent is Brandt. Applied to the boat launch, it would say stop supporting the launch, a result Brandt plainly rejects. That inconsistency is the whole method.
The columnist accepts the figures and even uses the same one for the launch. Nothing questions their accuracy.
choices.example: Example of this method: The councilor says one in twenty residents golfs, but the survey he cites counted only weekday players.

choices.note: Tempting, because the columnist does say the case isn’t made. But the columnist stops there and never says the subsidy should continue. Overstated conclusion.
choices.example: Example of this method: No one has proven the program is wasteful, so we should keep funding it.

questions.stimulus: Historian: It is often said that the weavers’ guild of medieval Varenna kept cloth prices high by restricting who could enter the trade. Guild records do show that the number of licensed weavers in Varenna fell by about a third between 1350 and 1400. But plague killed roughly a third of the city’s population during those same decades. So the drop in the number of licensed weavers ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the historian’s argument?
choices: suggests that the guild enforced its restrictions on entry less strictly after 1350 than before
resulted from deaths from plague rather than from any restriction on entry imposed by the guild
is about what one would expect even if the guild had admitted new weavers as freely as before
confirms that the guild’s restrictions on entry kept cloth prices in Varenna high during that period
was smaller than the drop in the number of people practicing most other trades in Varenna
questions.explanation: Weavers fell by about a third, and so did the whole population, so the weavers’ share of the city barely moved; that is just what an unchanged guild policy would produce, which is (C). (B) is the trap: it pushes the historian’s point too far, since showing the drop needs no guild explanation doesn’t show the guild played no part in it.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Popular view: the guild kept cloth prices high by restricting entry; 2. Licensed weavers fell by about a third from 1350 to 1400; 3. Plague killed about a third of the city’s population in the same decades.

breakdown.analysis: So the weavers fell by a third. So did everyone. Is that evidence of a guild policy? No: if the guild had changed nothing, you’d expect the weavers to shrink right along with the city. The share of residents who were weavers stayed about the same. It’s a count-versus-rate point: a falling count means nothing if the base fell just as much. The blank should say the drop is no evidence of restriction. (C) says exactly that, in a roundabout way: it’s what you’d see even under an open-door policy. Most students pick (B) because it sounds like the historian’s point. It fails because it’s too strong: the historian shows the evidence is neutral, not that plague was the whole story. The guild could still have restricted entry while the plague did the visible damage.

choices.note: Unsupported. Nothing compares how strictly the guild enforced anything before and after 1350. The numbers fit an unchanged policy.

Tempting, and it’s the trap. It takes the historian’s point and turns it up too far. Matching drops show the weaver count is no evidence of restriction, not that the guild had no effect at all. Restriction and plague could both have played a part.

CORRECT. If the guild had let weavers in as freely as before, the trade would still shrink by about a third, because the city did. So the drop is what an unchanged policy predicts, which means it can’t show a restriction.
Backwards. This is the popular view the historian is pushing against. The argument takes evidence away from it.
New information. Other trades are never mentioned, so there’s nothing to compare.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Barn owls, which prey heavily on voles, became considerably more numerous in the Brenna grasslands last year. Yet the grasslands’ vole population grew substantially over that same year. It follows that the voles there had more food available to them last year than they had the year before.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If voles have more food available in a year than in the year before, their population grows that year even if their predators increase.
A vole population cannot grow in a year in which barn owls in its area become more numerous unless some other condition affecting the voles improves that year.
Whether a vole population grows depends more on the food available to it than on the number of predators that hunt it.
The vole population of the Brenna grasslands would have grown even more last year if barn owls there had not become more numerous.
When the food available to a vole population does not increase, any rise in the number of its predators keeps that population from growing.
questions.explanation: The premises give a predator increase plus population growth; the conclusion adds food. (E) says no food increase plus a predator increase means no growth; since there was growth with a predator increase, its contrapositive yields more food. (B) is the trap: it reuses “barn owls” and the “unless” structure, but “some other condition” need not be food, so the conclusion does not follow. (A) runs the needed link backward.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Voles in the grasslands had more food last year than the year before.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Barn owls (vole predators) increased last year; the vole population grew anyway.

breakdown.analysis: Food appears only in the conclusion, so the bridge has to bring it in. The premises give: predators up AND population grew. We need a rule that turns that into “more food.” Rule: predators up AND no more food → no growth. Contrapositive: growth AND predators up → more food. That’s exactly our case. The right answer is written in that first, negative form, which makes it hard to spot. Most students pick (B) because it mentions barn owls and has the “unless” shape you’re hunting for. It fails because “some other condition” is broader than food: fewer foxes or a mild winter would satisfy it.

choices.note: This reverses the link. More food → growth. But we know about the growth and want to prove the food; this rule only runs from food to growth. Classic reversal.

Tempting, and it’s the trap. Predators up AND growth → some other condition improved. But which condition? Fewer foxes, a mild winter, less disease would all fit. It never pins it on food, so the conclusion still doesn’t follow.
A comparison of importance, not a rule. Even if food matters more than predators, the population could grow with steady food, say because the owls barely affected it. Doesn’t force more food.
Even if true, it says nothing about food. The population could have grown without any change in food. Not sufficient.
CORRECT. No more food + more predators → no growth. Contrapositive: growth + more predators → more food. The voles grew while the owls increased, so the food increased. The conclusion follows.

questions.stimulus: Lake manager: Large fish die-offs in Orren Lake have only two causes: water that is too low in oxygen, or toxins released by blooms of blue-green algae. Throughout last month’s die-off, our staff measured the lake’s oxygen at several depths daily on their afternoon rounds, and every reading was well within the normal range. The die-off, therefore, must have been caused by algal toxins.
questions.stem: The lake manager’s argument is flawed in that it
choices: fails to establish that the oxygen readings reflect conditions at the depths where the lake’s fish actually live
treats the fact that algal toxins are capable of causing a die-off as sufficient evidence that they caused this one
infers that algal toxins caused the die-off without offering any evidence that an algal bloom occurred last month
takes for granted that low oxygen and algal toxins are the only possible causes of a large die-off in the lake
overlooks the possibility that a condition absent whenever it was checked was nonetheless present during the period in question
questions.explanation: Oxygen was measured only on afternoon rounds, but a lake’s oxygen typically falls lowest at night and dawn, so normal afternoon readings do not rule out low oxygen. (E) describes this without naming oxygen or afternoons. (A) is the trap for skimmers: the readings were taken at several depths, so depth is covered and the gap is time. (B) and (C) describe flaws an elimination argument does not commit: with only two possible causes, ruling one out is the evidence for the other. (D) objects to a stated premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The die-off was caused by algal toxins.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Only two causes: low oxygen or algal toxins; oxygen was checked each afternoon and was always normal.

breakdown.analysis: Is the structure bad? No: two options, rule one out, the other is left. That’s valid. So attack the ruling out. Where were the readings taken? At several depths, so that’s covered. When? Only on the afternoon rounds. Lake oxygen typically bottoms out at night or dawn. A reading that’s normal at 3 p.m. doesn’t mean it was normal at 4 a.m. We need an answer that says the checks could have missed a low. The right answer says it abstractly: something absent whenever it was checked could still have been there. Most students pick (A) because it’s the familiar “wrong place” sampling objection; it fails because the stimulus already says several depths. (B) and (C) are the other pulls: each sounds like a missing step, but with only two possible causes, eliminating one is all the evidence the other needs.

choices.note: Tempting, and it’s the trap. It’s the classic “measured in the wrong place” objection, and it borrows the stimulus’s words. But the staff measured at several depths. The sampling gap here is about time, not place.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The surface water was clear, so the whole lake must be clean.

choices.note: Tempting, because inferring “did” from “can” is a real flaw. But the argument doesn’t rely on toxins merely being able to cause die-offs. It rules out the only other cause. If that ruling out worked, the conclusion would follow.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Raccoons can tip over trash cans, so a raccoon must have tipped over ours.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a missing piece. But the argument works by elimination: if there are only two possible causes and one is ruled out, the other must be the cause. No separate bloom evidence is needed. The problem is whether low oxygen was really ruled out.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The paint is peeling, so the walls must be damp, though no one has measured the moisture.

choices.note: A premise objection. The manager states this as fact, and the argument is entitled to it. LSAT flaw answers describe the move from premises to conclusion, not whether a premise is true.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Only two people had keys, so one of them must have taken the money, though others may have had keys.

choices.note: CORRECT. The condition is low oxygen. It was absent every time staff checked, on afternoon rounds, but oxygen could have dropped at night or early morning. If so, low oxygen wasn’t ruled out, and the elimination fails.

questions.stimulus: Every beekeeper who belongs to the Alder Valley cooperative sells honey at the town’s Saturday market. Some of the cooperative’s beekeepers also make candles from the wax their own hives produce. Hence, some people who make candles from the wax of their own hives sell honey at the Saturday market.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
