choices: Every guide at the Bastow Museum has a degree in art history. Some people with degrees in art history teach at the university. Hence, some guides at the Bastow Museum teach at the university.

Most of the employees of the Pratt Bakery work early-morning shifts during the week. Some of the bakery’s employees are university students. Hence, some university students work early-morning shifts at the Pratt Bakery.
Some volunteers at the Kessel Public Library are retired, and none of its volunteers has lived in Kessel County for under a year. Hence, some retirees have lived in the county for at least a year.

All of the moths in the Ilse collection were caught in Brazil, and all moths caught in Brazil for that collection were caught before 1950. Hence, all of the moths in the Ilse collection were caught before 1950.

Every licensed mountain guide in the town of Tarvik is certified in wilderness first aid. Some people certified in wilderness first aid work as lifeguards. Hence, some lifeguards are licensed mountain guides in Tarvik.
questions.explanation: The argument runs: all A are B; some A are C; so some C are B. (C) matches once you reorder its premises and read “none has lived there for under a year” as “all have lived there at least a year.” (B) is the trap: it copies the original sentence by sentence but opens with “most,” which breaks the validity, and (D) is valid but has an all-all-all shape.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some people who make candles from their own hives’ wax sell honey at the Saturday market.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every cooperative beekeeper sells honey at the market; some cooperative beekeepers make candles from their own wax.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; some A are C; so some C are B (valid).

breakdown.analysis: Is the original valid? Yes. Take the candle-making co-op members: they’re co-op members, so they sell honey. That gives you people who make candles and sell honey. We need another valid argument with the same skeleton: all A are B, some A are C, so some C are B. Translate before you compare: the match may scramble the order or state the “all” in negative form. (C) does both: it puts the “some” first, and “none has lived there for under a year” is just “all have lived there at least a year.” Most students pick (B) because it copies the original line for line. It fails on one word: “most” instead of “every.” The students could all be in the minority who don’t work early shifts, so (B)’s conclusion doesn’t follow.

choices.note: Invalid. All guides have art-history degrees, and some degree holders teach. But the teachers could be different degree holders. The shared term never links the two groups.

Tempting, because it copies the original line for line. But it starts with “most,” not “every.” The students could all be in the minority who don’t work early, so the conclusion doesn’t follow. The original is valid; this one isn’t.

CORRECT. Reorder it: no volunteer has lived in the county under a year, so every volunteer has lived there at least a year (all A are B). Some volunteers are retired (some A are C). So some retirees have lived there at least a year (some C are B). Same skeleton, same validity.
Valid, which makes it tempting, but the skeleton differs: all A are B, all B are C, so all A are C. No “some” premise and no “some” conclusion.
Invalid, for the same reason as (A): the first-aid group is the shared term, and the lifeguards may be first-aiders who aren’t guides.

questions.stimulus: By closing the steepest of its three trails to the Raven Gorge overlook two years ago and directing hikers to the other two, Fenmark National Park has made hiking to the overlook safer. Since the closure, the number of injuries reported on the overlook trails has fallen by 40 percent, even though the number of hikers using them has not declined.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Since the closure, the park has left unstaffed the ranger post where hikers from all three overlook trails used to report most of their injuries.
The two remaining trails are considerably longer than the steep trail was, so hikers now spend more time on the trails.
Hikers who once used the steep trail have crowded onto the other two trails, which are now noticeably more congested than before.
Some of the injuries reported on the remaining trails since the closure have been serious enough that hikers had to be carried out.
Before the closure, most of the injuries reported on the overlook trails were minor sprains rather than serious falls.
questions.explanation: The evidence is a drop in reported injuries. If the post where most injuries used to be reported is no longer staffed, reports could fall while injuries do not, so (A) undercuts the evidence itself. (C) sounds damaging, but injuries fell despite the crowding, so it does not weaken; (D) mentions serious injuries but only says some occurred, which is compatible with the trails being safer; (E) describes only injuries before the closure; (B) strengthens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Closing the steep trail made hiking to the overlook safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the closure, reported injuries on the overlook trails are down 40 percent with no drop in hikers.

breakdown.analysis: What exactly fell? Not injuries: reported injuries. A drop in reports can mean fewer injuries, or it can mean fewer of them get reported. If something about the closure made reporting harder, the 40 percent drop could be partly or wholly an artifact. We need an answer that drives a wedge between the reported number and the real one, or shows the real danger rose. Watch the answers that sound bad for the trails (crowding, serious injuries): check whether they actually cut against the conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. Hard to like, because it’s about a ranger post, not about the trails. But the argument rests on reported injuries. If the place where most injuries got reported is now unstaffed, reports can fall even if injuries don’t. The 40 percent drop may not mean the trails got safer.
Tempting, because it seems to change the picture. But read it: hikers spend more time on the trails and still get hurt less. That makes the drop more impressive. It strengthens.
Tempting, and it’s a trap. Crowding sounds dangerous. But the injury count fell even with the crowding, so this doesn’t show the trails are less safe; if anything it makes the drop more impressive.

Tempting, because serious injuries are the right worry. But “some” serious injuries is compatible with far fewer and less serious injuries overall. Without a comparison to before the closure, it can’t show things got worse.

Tempting, because it raises severity. But it describes only the injuries before the closure. It tells you nothing about whether today’s injuries are worse, so it can’t show the trails got more dangerous.

passages.title: Shaw’s stage directions
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Readers who open a play by George Bernard Shaw expecting the clipped notations of a working script are soon disabused. Before the first line of dialogue in Candida, Shaw describes not only the room in the parsonage where the action unfolds but the surrounding district of London, and then devotes a long paragraph to the clergyman at the play’s center: his age, his bearing, his politics, and the convictions that drive him, much of which no actor could display simply by walking onstage. Some critics have treated such passages as residue from Shaw’s apprenticeship as a novelist (he wrote five novels between 1879 and 1883 before turning to the theater) and so as evidence that he never fully trusted dialogue to do a dramatist’s work.

That reading overlooks the circumstances in which the directions were written. Shaw had begun his first play in the mid-1880s, but the London stage of the following decade offered him little. His early plays reached it, when they reached it at all, in short runs or private performances, and the official censor refused a license to Mrs Warren’s Profession, which could not be performed publicly in Britain for decades. In 1898 Shaw took his case to readers instead, publishing seven plays in two volumes as Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant. The acting editions of the day, whose directions were a shorthand of entrances and exits meant for stage managers, were all but unreadable by anyone else; Shaw set out to make a printed play something a person might read as readily as a novel.

Yet the directions are not novelistic in the way the critics suppose. A novel’s narrator ordinarily supplies a world to which the reader has no other access. Shaw’s directions describe a world that a theater could also present, and they are written with that fact in view: beside the commentary on a character’s temperament stand exact indications of furniture, light, and position that a director could follow to the letter. What the commentary adds is Shaw’s own reading of what a performance would show: his judgment of the people he has created, frequently ironic and sometimes openly at odds with the way those people see themselves.

Seen this way, the directions are of a piece with Shaw’s other work as a controversialist, the prefaces, pamphlets, and letters to newspapers in which he argued his positions throughout his life. A dramatist who wanted the theater to be a place of argument could hardly be content to let actors and audiences reach their own conclusions unassisted, and the printed play gave him a second stage on which the author could speak in his own voice. He went on writing such directions long after theater managers had become eager to produce his plays.

passages.title: Liquidated damages and the penalty doctrine
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
When contracting parties foresee that a breach would cause losses that are hard to measure, they often agree in advance on the sum the breaching party will pay. Courts enforce such liquidated damages clauses within limits. American courts generally uphold a stipulated sum that was a reasonable forecast of the harm a breach would cause, and they strike down as a penalty a sum so large that its evident function is to compel performance rather than to compensate; the injured party must then prove its actual damages in the ordinary way. In 2015 the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom recast the English rule, asking not whether a sum estimated the likely loss but whether it was out of all proportion to any legitimate interest the injured party had in the contract’s performance.

Even in reformed versions, the penalty doctrine is, according to the legal scholar Anselm Rudd, a relic. Courts enforce a contract, he notes, because its terms reflect what the parties judged to be in their interest, and a party that agrees to pay a large fixed sum for breach presumably receives something in exchange: a higher price, a faster schedule, or the contract itself, which the other side might otherwise have refused. Striking down the clause after the fact deprives the injured party of what it bargained for and hands the breaching party a benefit it never paid for. Rudd would therefore enforce any damages clause agreed to by commercial parties of comparable sophistication, however large the sum.

There is something to this: between well-advised firms, a court that second-guesses a negotiated figure may be substituting its own judgment of risk for theirs. The difficulty is that Rudd’s argument presupposes that the figure was in fact negotiated. Large firms routinely contract on standard forms that neither side reads closely, and a damages clause buried in such a form may reflect no one’s considered judgment at all. Rudd’s test of comparable sophistication describes the parties, not the transaction.

Nor are the signatories the only ones affected. A firm that must pay many times its counterparty’s actual loss may be unable to pay its other creditors or its employees; when a maker of hospital equipment owes a crushing sum for a two-week delay, the cost falls partly on those who depend on its continued operation. None of this revives the doctrine’s traditional rationale, which treated penalties as objectionable simply because they coerce performance. On that point Rudd is right, and the 2015 decision itself declined to treat a deterrent purpose as disqualifying. What the doctrine can still protect is the integrity of bargaining and the interests of those outside the contract. A court guided by those purposes would ask whether a disputed sum was actually bargained over and who besides the breaching party would bear it: harder questions than whether a figure fairly forecast the harm, the American test’s chief concern, but the ones on which the case for keeping the doctrine now rests.

passages.title: Probate inventories and the industrious revolution
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

For much of the early modern period, the material lives of ordinary households in England and the Netherlands left little trace in writing. Few such households kept diaries, and fewer still kept accounts. When a property holder died, however, appraisers, often neighbors of the deceased, commonly drew up a probate inventory: a list, often room by room, of the movable goods in the house, with a value beside each. Thousands survive, and historians who have tabulated them find that from the mid-seventeenth to the mid-eighteenth century, goods such as earthenware dishes, clocks, mirrors, and printed books appear in a growing share of households, including many of modest means.

The economic historian Jan de Vries has argued that this pattern cannot be explained by rising pay, since the best available wage series show little sustained improvement in laborers’ real wages over the period. He proposes instead what he calls an “industrious revolution”: households reallocated their time, with women and children in particular devoting more hours to work for the market, such as spinning and other piecework, and fewer to making things for the household’s own use. The added earnings went to goods that could be bought rather than made; the desire for such goods, on his account, was a cause of the harder work and not merely its reward. The lengthening lists of goods thus record a decision, made household by household, to work longer in order to buy more.

Whatever one makes of that interpretation, the inventories offer something no other source can: a systematic record of objects, compiled by eyewitnesses, across thousands of ordinary homes.

Passage B

Historians of everyday life have understandably seized on probate inventories, which record what diaries and account books rarely do: the ordinary contents of ordinary homes. But the impression of completeness these documents give is misleading.

To begin with, inventories were not taken for everyone. The poorest, whose possessions hardly justified the cost of appraisal, were seldom inventoried at all, so a household of “modest means” in a body of inventories is modest only by comparison with others who owned enough to be counted.

The people inventoried were also disproportionately old. A typical decedent had spent decades accumulating goods, so an inventory records a lifetime’s acquisitions rather than the habits of any one moment, and an apparent rise in ownership may partly reflect changes in who lived long enough to leave an inventory, and at what age.

Finally, appraisers often lumped cheap items together as “sundries,” and the point at which an object seemed worth listing separately depended on the appraiser and changed over time. An object’s first appearance in a series of inventories may therefore mark only a shift in what appraisers thought worth a separate entry. Historians who would trace changes in consumption must first correct for each of these distortions, mostly with evidence from outside the inventories.

passages.title: Bitter nectar
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Nectar is usually understood as a payment: a plant offers sugar so that animals will carry its pollen from flower to flower. It is therefore puzzling that the nectar of many plants also contains compounds that are bitter or toxic, such as nicotine in the nectar of some tobacco species or the grayanotoxins that make honey from certain rhododendrons poisonous to people. Biologists have proposed that the compounds may deter nectar thieves, insects that drink without transferring pollen; they may keep yeasts and bacteria from spoiling the nectar; they may screen out visitors that pollinate poorly; or they may do nothing useful in the nectar at all, having evolved to defend the leaves and seeped into the nectar.

A further proposal holds that they act on pollinators by shortening visits. Many plants bear numerous flowers at once, and a bee that finds sweet nectar tends to work its way through flower after flower on the same plant. Each such move carries pollen between the plant’s own flowers, and the seeds that result are inbred and frequently fail. A bee put off by bitter nectar takes a sip or two and, still hungry, flies on to another plant. Suppose a bee arrives carrying pollen from a distant plant. If it visits eight flowers, most of the pollen it leaves on the later ones will be the plant’s own, picked up from the earlier ones; if it visits only two, nearly all the pollen it leaves will be foreign.

One field experiment tested this proposal on a meadow perennial pollinated chiefly by bumblebees, whose nectar naturally contains a bitter alkaloid and whose likeliest thieves, ants, seldom climb its stalks. Researchers replaced the nectar of some plants with a sugar solution containing the alkaloid at its natural concentration and that of others with the same solution lacking it. Bees on the alkaloid-free plants visited markedly more flowers per plant, and genetic markers showed that a larger share of the seeds from the alkaloid plants had been sired by other plants. That is the outcome the visit-shortening proposal predicts, and with thieves scarce, deterring them could not have produced it.

Much remains open, however. Tracing the parentage of seeds does not count them, and flowers that departing bees skip may go unpollinated. In a dense stand a departing bee easily reaches another plant of the same species; where plants grow sparsely, it might as readily turn to another species, carrying the pollen where it can fertilize nothing. Nor does an effect on pollinators reveal how the trait arose. A compound that first entered nectar as a by-product of leaf defense could have been retained for its effect on visits, and one that shortens visits might also protect the nectar from microbes. Several of the explanations may hold true of a single compound, and the better question may be not which is right but how much each contributes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Shaw’s long stage directions show that his training as a novelist left him unwilling to rely on dialogue alone to convey his characters.
The commentary in Shaw’s stage directions was a deliberate means of addressing the readers of his plays directly, in keeping with his other polemical writing.
Shaw’s stage directions are better understood as a response to a stage closed to him by censorship than as a holdover from his career as a novelist.
Although Shaw’s stage directions are often dismissed as novelistic, they are more precise as instructions for production than those of any other dramatist of his time.
Shaw’s stage directions were meant chiefly to guide directors, and their commentary was intended to help actors interpret characters whose motives the dialogue leaves unclear.
questions.explanation: The author rejects the critics’ view that the directions are a novelist’s leftover habit and argues that the commentary is Shaw speaking to readers in his own voice, like his prefaces and pamphlets. That is B. C has the same “better seen as X than as Y” shape as a good main point and rejects the right view, but it puts necessity in Shaw’s place: the last sentence says he kept writing such directions after managers were eager to stage his plays, so the closed stage can’t be the whole story.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall claim about Shaw’s stage directions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The critics’ view is in the last sentence of the first paragraph; the rebuttal opens the second paragraph; the author’s own account fills the third and fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Whose view is the passage built around? The critics say the directions are novelist’s residue. The author says no: they were written for readers when the stage was closed (paragraph 2), they aren’t really novelistic (paragraph 3), and they belong with Shaw’s polemics (paragraph 4). Prephrase: the commentary was Shaw’s deliberate way of talking to readers himself. Most students who miss this pick (C), because it looks like a classic main-point answer: it names the critics’ view and replaces it. But it replaces it with the wrong thing. The censorship history is one paragraph’s point, and the last sentence (he kept writing these directions once theaters wanted his plays) shows necessity isn’t the explanation. Don’t pick an answer for its shape.

choices.note: This is the critics’ view from the first paragraph, which the author rejects.

CORRECT. Deliberate (written for readers, not out of habit), in Shaw’s own voice (the “second stage”), and of a piece with his prefaces and pamphlets (fourth paragraph). A plain statement of the thesis.

Tempting: the right target and the right shape. But the replacement view is wrong. Censorship is the second paragraph’s occasion, and the last sentence says Shaw kept writing such directions long after managers were eager to produce his plays, so a closed stage can’t be the account the author offers.
Too strong. The author notes that the directions include exact staging indications, but never compares Shaw’s precision with every other dramatist’s.

Wrong audience. The passage says the commentary is a “reading” of the performance for readers of the printed play, not guidance for actors. The precise staging notes are for directors, but they aren’t the commentary.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the acting editions of plays that were available when Shaw published Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant
choices: were meant for the reading public but proved too technical for most readers to follow
were addressed chiefly to actors and gave guidance on how each role should be interpreted
had been revised by their authors in order to make them more accessible to ordinary readers
used a technical notation that served those who staged plays but few others
supplied the exact indications of furniture, light, and position that Shaw later adopted
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the acting editions’ directions “were a shorthand of entrances and exits meant for stage managers” and “all but unreadable by anyone else.” D says the same in other words. A is the closest trap: the editions were indeed hard for readers to follow, but they were never meant for readers. B gets the audience and the content wrong (actors and interpretation, not stage managers and entrances and exits).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the acting editions of Shaw’s day.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph, second-to-last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Locate it: “The acting editions of the day, whose directions were a shorthand of entrances and exits meant for stage managers, were all but unreadable by anyone else.” Prephrase: technical shorthand, useful to the people running a production, useless to readers. Watch for answers that keep the “unreadable” half but change who the editions were for.

choices.note: The near-miss. It gets the result right (ordinary readers couldn’t follow them) but the purpose wrong: the passage says the directions were “meant for stage managers,” not for the reading public. Making plays readable was Shaw’s aim, not the acting editions’ failed one.
Tempting, since it says the editions were for theater people. But the passage says stage managers, and the content was entrances and exits, not advice on interpreting roles.
The opposite. They were “all but unreadable” by ordinary readers; making plays readable was Shaw’s project, not theirs.
CORRECT. “Shorthand” = technical notation; “meant for stage managers” and “unreadable by anyone else” = served those who staged plays but few others.
This borrows words from the third paragraph, where the exact indications of furniture, light, and position are Shaw’s own. Nothing says he took them from the acting editions.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Shaw’s practice of writing extended commentary into his stage directions can most accurately be described as
choices: amused tolerance of a personal eccentricity
reluctant acceptance of a necessary compromise
appreciation tempered by doubts about its value in actual performance
approval of it as a purposeful and fitting choice
detached interest in its historical origins
questions.explanation: The author presents the practice as a response to real conditions, says it gave Shaw “a second stage” for his own voice, and ties it to his aims as a controversialist; nothing in the passage criticizes it. That is approval: D. C is the reflex answer for attitude questions, but the author voices no doubts about the directions’ value in performance; the third paragraph says they include indications a director “could follow to the letter” and that the commentary is Shaw’s “own reading of what a performance would show.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how the author feels about Shaw’s habit of putting commentary into his directions.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The author’s voice runs through the second to fourth paragraphs; look for evaluative words.

breakdown.analysis: Collect the author’s words: the critics’ reading “overlooks the circumstances,” the printed play is “a second stage on which the author could speak in his own voice,” and the practice is “of a piece with” his lifelong controversy. Is there any “but” aimed at Shaw? No; the only target is the critics. So the attitude is plain approval. Many test-takers pick (C) out of habit, because so many LSAT authors are “positive with a reservation.” Check the reservation: is there one here? There isn’t. You can’t pick an attitude from a template; it has to be in the text.

choices.note: Nothing is played for amusement, and the author treats the practice as deliberate, not an eccentricity.
Half right on the history (paragraph 2 describes the necessity), but the author isn’t reluctant, and the last sentence says Shaw kept it up after the necessity had passed.

Tempting, because “appreciation tempered by doubts” is a common correct answer on real tests. Here, though, the author expresses no doubt about the directions in performance; the third paragraph stresses that they are written with performance in view.
CORRECT. “Purposeful” matches the deliberate choice described in the second paragraph; “fitting” matches the fourth paragraph’s claim that the practice served Shaw’s aims as a controversialist.
The author isn’t detached; the passage argues for a view of the directions and against the critics.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: challenge a characterization of Shaw’s directions by contrasting what they do with what the narration in a novel typically does
concede that Shaw’s directions resemble a novelist’s narration before arguing that the resemblance was forced on him by the theatrical conditions of his time
show that Shaw’s directions were written primarily for directors and only secondarily for those who would read the published plays
explain what led the critics mentioned in the first paragraph to mistake Shaw’s directions for a holdover from his years as a novelist
argue that the commentary in Shaw’s directions misrepresents his characters by contradicting the way they see themselves
questions.explanation: The third paragraph opens “Yet the directions are not novelistic in the way the critics suppose” and then sets a novel’s narrator (who supplies a world readers can’t otherwise reach) against Shaw’s directions (which describe a stageable world and add a reading of it). That is A. D is the near-miss: the paragraph answers the critics, but by refuting their label, not by explaining what led them to it. B runs the second paragraph’s history into the third and invents a concession.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the third paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, especially its first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Topic sentence first: “the directions are not novelistic in the way the critics suppose.” Then the contrast: a narrator supplies a world you can’t otherwise reach; Shaw’s directions describe a world a theater could also present, and the commentary is a reading of it. So: rebut the “novelistic” label by contrasting Shaw’s directions with real narration. Rebutting a view is not the same as explaining why people held it; that difference is what (D) hopes you miss.

choices.note: CORRECT. The characterization is the critics’ “novelistic” label, and the paragraph challenges it by contrasting the directions with a narrator’s usual job.
The conditions of the theater are the second paragraph’s topic, and the third paragraph concedes nothing; it denies that the directions are novelistic in the critics’ sense.
Too strong. The paragraph says the directions include instructions a director could follow, but it doesn’t rank directors above readers; the commentary is aimed at readers.

The near-miss. The paragraph does take on the critics, but it argues that they are wrong, by showing how the directions differ from narration; it never says what led them to their view. (If anything, the first paragraph’s length of description is what invites the mistake.)
This reuses the passage’s words but flips the evaluation. Shaw’s commentary disagrees with how the characters see themselves; the author presents that as Shaw’s judgment, not as a misrepresentation.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the commentary on characters in Shaw’s stage directions (third paragraph)?
choices: It describes a world to which readers would otherwise have no access, much as the narration of a novel does.
It was added to the published plays only after the censor had refused to license them for public performance.
It can express a view of a character that the character, as the play presents him or her, would not share.
It is less exact than the indications of furniture, light, and position that accompany it, and so is of little use to directors.
It was meant to be read aloud to actors so that they could convey Shaw’s judgment of each character in performance.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph calls the commentary Shaw’s own judgment of his characters, “sometimes openly at odds with the way those people see themselves.” C restates that abstractly. A is the trap: it repeats the third paragraph’s description of what a novel’s narrator does, which the author contrasts with Shaw’s directions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim about the commentary that the author would endorse.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What does the author say the commentary is? “Shaw’s own reading of what a performance would show: his judgment of the people he has created, frequently ironic and sometimes openly at odds with the way those people see themselves.” So the commentary can say things about a character that the character wouldn’t agree with. Most students who miss this pick (A), because it uses the passage’s own language. But that language describes what a novel’s narrator does, and the whole point of the paragraph is that Shaw’s directions differ from it.

choices.note: Tempting: these are the third paragraph’s words. But they describe a novel’s narrator, and the author says Shaw’s directions describe “a world that a theater could also present.” The author would reject this.
No timing is given. The passage says the plays were published in 1898 after the censor’s refusal, but not that the commentary was added only then.
CORRECT. “openly at odds with the way those people see themselves” means Shaw’s judgment of a character can be one the character wouldn’t accept.
The passage mentions the exact staging indications, but never ranks them against the commentary or says the commentary is of little use; it’s aimed at readers, not directors.
Nothing about reading directions aloud to actors. The commentary is a reading of the play for the reader of the printed text.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the role that, according to the author, the commentary in Shaw’s printed stage directions plays?
choices: A choreographer publishes a detailed notation of her ballet so that companies unable to consult her can reproduce every one of its movements exactly.
A filmmaker records a commentary track, offered to home viewers with the film, giving her own often skeptical judgments of the characters as their scenes play.
A playwright publishes, with the text of her play, an essay explaining the political convictions that led her to write it and that she hopes readers will share.
A playwright gives each actor, at the first rehearsal, a private account of the character’s history that the play itself never reveals to the audience.
A composer writes program notes describing the historical events that inspired her symphony, so that listeners in the concert hall can recognize each of the episodes it depicts.
questions.explanation: In the third and fourth paragraphs the commentary is the author’s own, often ironic judgment of the characters, delivered alongside a work that can be fully staged without it, on a “second stage” where the author speaks in his own voice. The commentary track in B matches every element. C is the closest trap: it gives a creator’s own voice to readers, like Shaw’s prefaces, but as a separate essay on her convictions rather than running judgment of the characters. D is private and for performers, and E supplies background facts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation that works the way the author says Shaw’s commentary works.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph’s last sentence and the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: List the elements: 1. the work can be performed complete without the commentary (the commentary is Shaw’s “own reading of what a performance would show”); 2. the commentary is the creator’s own judgment of the characters, often ironic; 3. it reaches the audience of a separate version (the printed play) alongside the work, a “second stage” for the author’s voice. The right answer must match all three. Watch for answers that match one or two. (C) is built to match the “own voice to readers” element and nothing else: it describes a preface, not commentary on the characters.

choices.note: Matches only the precise-instruction side of Shaw’s directions. It has no commentary or judgment at all.

CORRECT. The film is complete without the track; the track is the filmmaker’s own, often skeptical, view of her characters; and it reaches viewers of a separate version alongside the work. That’s Shaw’s “second stage.”

The near-miss. It is the creator speaking to readers in her own voice, much like the prefaces the fourth paragraph mentions. But it is a separate essay about her convictions, not commentary that runs alongside the action giving her judgment of the characters, which is the role the question asks about.
Tempting, because a creator gives extra material about characters. But it is private and for actors, not readers, and it is background history, not the creator’s judgment.
Close, but program notes supply background facts so listeners can follow the work; Shaw’s commentary gives his opinion of the people in the play.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The penalty doctrine should be abolished, because a court that refuses to enforce a negotiated sum substitutes its own judgment of risk for that of the parties.
Although Rudd’s case for abolishing the penalty doctrine fails, the doctrine’s traditional concern with coercing performance remains the soundest reason for keeping it.
Courts should enforce damages clauses between commercial parties of comparable sophistication, since such parties can judge their own risks better than a court can.
Because damages clauses in commercial contracts seldom reflect genuine bargaining, courts should scrutinize every such clause closely before enforcing it.
Although Rudd rightly holds that coercing performance is not objectionable in itself, the penalty doctrine should be kept for other purposes, which should guide its application.
questions.explanation: The author grants Rudd one point (coercion alone isn’t objectionable), rejects his call for abolition, and grounds the doctrine in bargaining integrity and outsiders’ interests, which should shape the questions a court asks. That is E. B has the same concessive shape and also rejects abolition, but it keeps the wrong reason: the author says the traditional coercion rationale is not revived.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position on the penalty doctrine and Rudd’s argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Rudd’s case is the second paragraph; the author’s replies are the third and fourth; the conclusion is the last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: So is the author for Rudd or against him? Both, on different points. 1. Rudd is right that coercing performance isn’t objectionable in itself (“On that point Rudd is right”). 2. But abolition is wrong, because the doctrine protects real bargaining and people outside the contract. 3. Those purposes tell a court what to ask. Prephrase: keep the doctrine, for new reasons, and let those reasons shape it. Most students who miss this pick (B), because it opens the same way the key does and rejects abolition. Read the second half: it rests the doctrine on its traditional concern with coercion, the one rationale the author says is not revived.

choices.note: Rudd’s view, not the author’s. The author concedes that courts may sometimes second-guess well-advised firms, but rejects abolition.
Tempting: concessive, balanced, anti-abolition. But “traditional concern with coercing performance” is exactly what the author drops: “None of this revives the doctrine’s traditional rationale.”
This is Rudd’s test, which the author faults: comparable sophistication “describes the parties, not the transaction.”
Too strong. The author’s worry is about clauses buried in forms nobody read and harm to outsiders, not about every clause.
CORRECT. The concession (Rudd is right about coercion), the rejection of abolition, and the new purposes that should guide application (the last two sentences).

questions.stem: According to the passage, the test adopted by the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom in 2015 differs from the test generally used by American courts in that the British test
choices: asks whether the stipulated sum was a reasonable forecast of the harm that a breach would be likely to cause
requires the injured party to prove its actual damages before any part of the stipulated sum can be recovered
permits courts to enforce any damages clause agreed to by commercial parties of comparable sophistication
weighs the stipulated sum against the injured party’s justifiable stake in the contract’s being carried out, not against the probable loss
treats any clause whose evident purpose is to discourage breach as a penalty, regardless of how large or small the stipulated sum is
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the 2015 decision asks “not whether a sum estimated the likely loss but whether it was out of all proportion to any legitimate interest the injured party had in the contract’s performance.” D paraphrases that contrast. A is the American test, swapped onto the wrong court.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how the 2015 British test differs from the American test.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two tests, side by side. American: was the sum a reasonable forecast of the harm? British (2015): is the sum out of all proportion to the injured party’s legitimate interest in performance? So the difference is the yardstick: likely loss versus legitimate interest in performance. Expect a trap that gives you the American yardstick.

choices.note: This is the American test (“a reasonable forecast of the harm”), the one the British court moved away from.
Proving actual damages is what happens after a clause is struck down, under either rule; it isn’t the British test.
That’s Rudd’s proposal, not the 2015 decision.

CORRECT. “Justifiable stake in seeing the contract carried out” = “legitimate interest ... in the contract’s performance”; “rather than the probable loss” = “not whether a sum estimated the likely loss.”
Backwards. The last paragraph says the 2015 decision “declined to treat a deterrent purpose as disqualifying.”

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, Rudd is described as holding that a party that agrees to pay a large fixed sum for breach
choices: is usually less sophisticated than the party that drafted the clause and so deserves the protection of the courts
should be held to that sum only if it can be shown to have received a higher price or a faster schedule in return
expects that a court will reduce the sum if a breach occurs and therefore agrees to the sum more readily
has in all likelihood obtained some advantage from the other side in return for accepting that obligation
would be deprived of what it bargained for if a court were to strike down the clause after the fact
questions.explanation: The second paragraph: such a party “presumably receives something in exchange: a higher price, a faster schedule, or the contract itself.” D paraphrases that. B borrows the passage’s examples but turns them into a condition Rudd never imposes; he would enforce such clauses “however large the sum” between comparable parties. E swaps the parties: it is the injured party, not the one who agreed to pay, that Rudd says is deprived of its bargain.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Rudd says about the party that agrees to a large damages sum.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Rudd: the promisor “presumably receives something in exchange” (a higher price, a faster schedule, or the contract itself). Prephrase: it probably got something for agreeing. Two traps reuse the passage’s words: one turns the examples into a requirement, and one takes a phrase about the other party.

choices.note: Rudd’s test assumes comparable sophistication; he says nothing about this party being weaker.

Tempting, because “a higher price, a faster schedule” are Rudd’s own examples. But they’re examples of what the party presumably gets, not conditions for enforcement; Rudd would enforce any such clause between comparable firms, and the exchange can even be “the contract itself.”
Nothing in Rudd’s argument concerns what the party expects courts to do.
CORRECT. “Presumably receives something in exchange” = “in all likelihood obtained some advantage ... in return.”
Wrong party. Rudd says striking the clause “deprives the injured party of what it bargained for”; the party that agreed to pay is the one that gets the unearned benefit.

questions.stem: In saying that Rudd’s test of comparable sophistication “describes the parties, not the transaction” (last sentence of the third paragraph), the author most likely means that the test
choices: looks to the size of the stipulated sum rather than to the loss that a breach actually caused
considers whether the parties were equally sophisticated but not whether the stipulated sum was proportionate to the likely loss
applies to contracts between two firms but not to contracts between a firm and a private individual
requires a court to examine each party’s private reasons for entering into the contract in the first place
asks what kind of firms made the agreement but not how the clause at issue got into it
questions.explanation: The third paragraph’s worry is that a clause “buried in” a standard form “may reflect no one’s considered judgment,” even between sophisticated firms. So the test looks at who the parties are, not at whether this clause was actually bargained over: E. B is the near-miss: Rudd’s test does ignore the size of the sum, but that isn’t the transaction-level fact the paragraph is about.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the phrase means in its context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, read from “The difficulty is” to the end.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentences before the phrase. The difficulty: Rudd presupposes the figure was negotiated, but sophisticated firms sign standard forms nobody reads, so a clause may reflect no one’s judgment. Then: the test “describes the parties, not the transaction.” So the parties = how sophisticated the firms are; the transaction = how this clause came to be in this deal. Most students who miss this pick (B), because it’s true that Rudd ignores proportionality (“however large the sum”). But the paragraph’s complaint is about negotiation, not size, and the phrase sums up that complaint.

choices.note: Rudd’s test doesn’t look at the sum at all; he’d enforce it “however large.”
Tempting. Rudd’s test really does ignore proportionality. But the phrase sums up the third paragraph’s point, which is about whether the clause was negotiated, not about its size.
No such distinction appears. The test is about comparable sophistication, not whether the parties are firms or individuals.
The opposite problem: the author’s complaint is that the test doesn’t look closely enough at the deal, not that it digs into private motives.
CORRECT. “The parties” = what kind of firms they are; “not the transaction” = not whether this particular clause was actually bargained over or slipped into a form.

questions.stem: The author mentions a maker of hospital equipment (second sentence of the last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate how a damages clause buried in a standard form can impose a sum that neither party actually considered
suggest that the penalty doctrine should apply with special force to firms whose products serve essential public needs
give a concrete instance of an enforced penalty’s burden falling on more than the two contracting parties
provide an example of a damages clause that reasonably estimated the harm that a brief delay would cause
show that a breach lasting only two weeks seldom causes the injured party a significant loss
questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that “the signatories” are not “the only ones affected”: a firm paying a crushing sum may be unable to pay creditors, employees, or suppliers, and the cost falls on those who depend on it. C states that purpose abstractly. B over-reads the example: hospital equipment makes the harm vivid, but the author never proposes a special rule for essential industries.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find why the author brings up the hospital-equipment maker.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before the example: “Nor are the signatories the only ones affected.” The example then shows a crushing penalty hurting people who depend on the firm. So its job is to make the outsider point concrete. (B) is the trap for readers who notice the hospital detail and inflate it into a policy. The author’s rule is about outsiders in general, not about one kind of industry.

choices.note: That is the third paragraph’s point about standard forms. The hospital example is about who bears the cost, not how the clause got there.
Tempting, because hospitals sound like a special case. But the author draws no special rule for essential industries; the example illustrates a general point about third parties.
CORRECT. The burden reaching “more than the two contracting parties” is exactly “Nor are the signatories the only ones affected.”
The example describes a “crushing sum,” many times the actual loss. That’s a penalty, not a reasonable estimate.
The passage says nothing about how much a two-week delay usually costs; the point is the size of the payment, not of the loss.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A legal rule and a recent revision of it are described, a scholar’s objection to the rule is presented, the revision is shown to answer that objection, and the rule’s abolition is rejected.

A legal rule is described, a scholar’s case against it is presented, two weaknesses in that case are identified, and the rule’s traditional rationale is reaffirmed as the best ground for retaining it.

A scholar’s proposal to reform a legal rule is presented, two objections to the proposal are raised, and the proposal is endorsed, with modifications, for contracts between sophisticated commercial parties only.
Two versions of a legal rule are compared, a scholar’s preference for one of the versions is criticized, and a compromise between the two versions is proposed.
A legal rule and a variant of it are described, a scholar’s case against the rule is set out, two shortcomings in that case are noted, and another rationale for the rule is advanced.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives the American rule and the 2015 British variant; paragraph 2 gives Rudd’s case for abolition; paragraphs 3 and 4 note two gaps (unnegotiated clauses, outsiders); the last two sentences ground the doctrine in different purposes. That is E. B matches every step but the last: the author says the traditional rationale is not revived.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the description that matches the passage’s sequence, step by step.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All four paragraphs; check each step against its paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. rule (American) plus variant (British 2015); 2. Rudd’s case for abolition; 3. gap one: the clause may not have been negotiated; 4. gap two: outsiders, then a new basis for the rule (bargaining integrity and outsiders). Organization answers die on one wrong element, so check every clause. (B) gets three of four steps right, which is why it pulls; its last step is the one thing the author explicitly rejects.

choices.note: The 2015 revision is never shown to answer Rudd. Rudd says even reformed versions are a relic, and the author answers him with other considerations.
Tempting, since the first three steps fit. But the last is wrong: “None of this revives the doctrine’s traditional rationale.” The author offers a different rationale.
Rudd’s proposal is abolition, not reform, and the author doesn’t endorse it for anyone.
The passage doesn’t compare the two versions to choose between them, and Rudd has no preference for either; he rejects both.
CORRECT. Rule and variant (paragraph 1), Rudd’s case (paragraph 2), two shortcomings (paragraphs 3 and 4), and a different rationale for keeping the rule (the last two sentences).

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if accepted, would most help to justify the position the author takes in the last two sentences of the passage?
choices: Courts should keep a power to override agreed terms, but should exercise it only insofar as doing so protects the process of agreement itself or people outside the agreement.
A court should refuse to enforce a stipulated sum whenever it far exceeds any loss a breach could plausibly cause, however carefully the sum was negotiated.
A court should enforce every damages clause agreed to by sophisticated commercial parties, unless paying the stipulated sum would leave the breaching party unable to meet its other debts in full.
A court should enforce any term to which both contracting parties freely agreed, unless one of them was induced to agree to it by fraud or by duress.
A court should refuse to enforce any contractual term whose evident purpose is to induce a party to perform rather than to compensate for a breach.
questions.explanation: The last two sentences say the doctrine should survive to protect the integrity of bargaining and outsiders, so a court should ask whether a sum was bargained over and who else would bear it. A, in abstract terms, says to keep the power and to use it for exactly those two purposes; accept it and the author’s position follows. B is the near-miss: it would justify keeping a penalty rule, but one keyed to the size of the sum “however carefully the sum was negotiated,” not to the questions the author wants asked. C keeps Rudd’s sophistication test and covers only outsiders.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the principle that, if accepted, would lead to keeping the penalty doctrine for the author’s two purposes.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: The position has two parts: 1. keep the doctrine (some clauses should still be refused); 2. apply it for its remaining purposes, the integrity of bargaining and the protection of outsiders, which means asking whether the sum was bargained over and who else bears it. A justifying principle has to deliver both: a reason to keep the power to refuse, and a rule that aims it at those two purposes. Test each choice by asking: if I accepted this, would I be pushed to the author’s view? (A) does it in abstract dress: “the process of agreement itself” is the bargaining concern, and “people outside the agreement” are the outsiders. Most students who miss this pick (B) or (C). (B) keeps a rule but ties it to the size of the sum, the forecast-style question the author calls easier but not the one that matters. (C) keeps Rudd’s sophistication test, which the author says can’t tell a negotiated clause from one nobody read, and covers only one of the two purposes.

choices.note: CORRECT. Keeping a power to override agreed terms rules out abolition. Using it “only insofar as” it protects “the process of agreement itself” (the integrity of bargaining: was the sum actually bargained over?) or “people outside the agreement” (who besides the breaching party would bear it?) points the doctrine at exactly the author’s two questions, and leaves out the coercion rationale the author drops.

Tempting, since it keeps a penalty rule. But it turns on the size of the sum “however carefully the sum was negotiated,” while the author wants courts to ask whether it was bargained over and who else would bear it.

Half a match. It protects some outsiders, but it adopts the sophistication test the author faults and ignores the bargaining concern, so it would enforce a crushing clause buried in a form nobody read.
This is close to Rudd’s position: enforce whatever was agreed, with the ordinary contract defenses. It supports abolition, not the author’s view.
This is the traditional rationale (coercion is objectionable), which the author says is not revived.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Courts should presume that any damages clause in a standard-form contract is unenforceable unless the party relying on it shows that it was actually negotiated.
The 2015 British decision erred in declining to treat a deterrent purpose as sufficient grounds for refusing to enforce a damages clause.
Rudd’s proposal would be acceptable if it were confined to damages clauses that both of the contracting parties had in fact negotiated.
That a damages clause was meant to pressure a party into performing does not alone show that a court should refuse to enforce it.
Damages clauses between large firms are less often the product of genuine bargaining than are those between individuals.
questions.explanation: In the last paragraph the author says the traditional rationale, which objected to penalties “simply because they coerce performance,” is not revived, and adds “On that point Rudd is right.” So pressure to perform is not, alone, a reason to refuse enforcement: D. C is the trap: limiting Rudd’s rule to negotiated clauses would answer the third paragraph’s objection, but not the fourth’s, since a negotiated penalty can still ruin creditors and employees.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author’s reasoning commits him or her to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph, read with the third.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase; test each choice against both of the author’s objections and the one concession. The concession is the key here: “None of this revives the doctrine’s traditional rationale, which treated penalties as objectionable simply because they coerce performance. On that point Rudd is right.” Put plainly: coercing performance isn’t enough to condemn a clause. (C) is the most tempting answer, because it fixes the gap the author spends a whole paragraph on. But the author raises a second gap: outsiders hurt by a crushing payment. A negotiated clause can still do that, so the author wouldn’t accept Rudd’s proposal even in that form.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says a clause buried in a form “may” reflect no one’s judgment; nothing supports a presumption against all such clauses.
Backwards. The author agrees that a deterrent purpose alone doesn’t condemn a clause, which is just what the 2015 decision held.
Tempting, since it answers the third paragraph’s objection. But the fourth paragraph’s objection, harm to outsiders, applies to negotiated clauses too, so the author would still reject the proposal.
CORRECT. The author rejects treating penalties as objectionable “simply because they coerce performance” and says Rudd is right on that point.
No comparison with individuals’ contracts appears anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: explaining why ordinary households acquired more goods during a period in which wages rose little
assessing what probate inventories can reveal about changes in the possessions of ordinary households
describing the procedures by which appraisers compiled probate inventories and assigned values to goods
evaluating de Vries’s explanation of why households came to devote more hours to work for the market
comparing the reliability of probate inventories with that of diaries and household account books
questions.explanation: Passage A reports what inventories show about rising ownership and why they are uniquely valuable; passage B argues that they show less about such changes than they seem to. Both are about what this kind of record can tell us: B. A and D concern only passage A’s account of de Vries, which passage B never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic both passages share.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first and last paragraphs of each passage.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: inventories show a rise in household goods; de Vries explains it; the inventories are uniquely valuable. Passage B: inventories look complete but aren’t, so they can’t settle whether households were buying more. Common ground: what inventories can and can’t tell us about changes in household possessions. Watch for answers that fit only one passage; (D) is the likeliest slip, since passage B’s doubts bear on de Vries without ever naming him.

choices.note: Only passage A explains the rise. Passage B never discusses wages or why households bought more.
CORRECT. Passage A says what inventories reveal (rising ownership, a unique record); passage B says how far they can be trusted to reveal it.
Both mention how inventories were made, but only as support; neither is mainly about procedure.
Tempting, because passage B’s doubts would bear on de Vries. But passage B never mentions him or his explanation, and passage A only reports it.
Both mention diaries and account books in passing, as sources that are scarce, but neither compares their reliability.

questions.stem: Passage B states which one of the following about the appraisers who compiled probate inventories?
choices: They were often neighbors of the person whose goods they listed.
They assigned higher values to the possessions of older decedents than to those of younger ones.
They did not all apply one fixed standard in deciding which goods merited an entry of their own.
They lumped cheap items together to reduce the cost of appraising the goods of poorer households.
They seldom recorded goods that had been acquired during the last years of the decedent’s life.
questions.explanation: Passage B’s last paragraph says the point at which an object seemed worth listing separately “depended on the appraiser and changed over time.” C says that without the passage’s words. A is true, but passage A says it, not passage B; D splices “sundries” with “the cost of appraisal,” which passage B uses about why the poorest weren’t inventoried at all.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage B itself says about appraisers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: The stem limits you to passage B. Its claim about appraisers: they lumped cheap items as “sundries,” and the threshold for a separate entry “depended on the appraiser and changed over time.” Prephrase: appraisers weren’t consistent about what got its own line. Two traps: (A) is in the wrong passage, and (D) glues together two of passage B’s phrases that answer different questions.

choices.note: Tempting, and true of inventories, but passage A says it (“appraisers, often neighbors of the deceased”). The stem asks what passage B states.
Passage B says older decedents had accumulated more, not that appraisers valued their goods more highly.
CORRECT. “Depended on the appraiser and changed over time” means there was no single, fixed standard for a separate entry.
This joins two different parts of passage B. “The cost of appraisal” explains why the poorest weren’t inventoried at all; lumping items as sundries is given no motive.
Passage B says an inventory records a lifetime’s acquisitions, not that recent purchases were left out.

questions.stem: In passage A, the reference to wage series (first sentence of the second paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: suggest that households of modest means were poorer than their inventories make them appear
show that the prices of earthenware and similar goods fell over the course of the period
help rule out one possible explanation of the pattern found in the inventories
illustrate the kinds of written records that ordinary households of the period usually kept
support the claim that inventories are more reliable than other sources of information about income
questions.explanation: De Vries argues that the spread of goods “cannot be explained by rising pay, since” the wage series show little improvement. The wage evidence removes the obvious explanation before he offers his own: C. A is passage B’s concern about “modest means,” not the job the wage series does in passage A.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find why passage A cites wage series.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the second paragraph of passage A.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence: the pattern “cannot be explained by rising pay, since the best available wage series show little sustained improvement.” The wage series knock out one explanation (higher pay) so de Vries can offer another (more work). Expect wrong answers that drift to passage B or invent a price claim.

choices.note: That’s closer to passage B’s point about “modest means.” In passage A, the wages bear on why goods spread, not on how poor households were.
Prices are never mentioned. The wage series concern pay, not the cost of goods.
CORRECT. Higher pay is the possible explanation; the flat wage series rule it out, clearing the way for the industrious revolution.
Wage series aren’t household records, and passage A says few households kept records at all.
Passage A never compares inventories and wage series as sources on income.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage B would be most likely to make regarding the statement in passage A that the goods appeared in households “of modest means”?
choices: Calling those households modest takes as its standard a group that leaves out many of the people least able to afford such goods.
Those households probably owned fewer of the goods than their inventories indicate, since appraisers listed even cheap objects individually.
Those households probably acquired most of their goods by inheritance rather than by purchase.
Those households were probably poorer than their inventories make them appear, because appraisers tended to set low values on the goods of humble decedents.
The goods probably reached those households only after they had already become common among the wealthy.
questions.explanation: Passage B’s second paragraph says the poorest were seldom inventoried, so a household of “modest means” in the inventories is modest “only by comparison with others who owned enough to be counted.” A states that criticism abstractly: the comparison group omits the poorest. D runs it backwards (passage B suggests such households were better off than the label implies, not poorer), and B misreads the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find passage B’s likely objection to the “modest means” claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B has a paragraph aimed squarely at this: the poorest weren’t inventoried, so “modest” in an inventory sample means modest among people well-off enough to be counted. Prephrase: the yardstick is skewed, because the bottom of society isn’t in the sample. The key says that without the passage’s words, which is why it’s easy to skim past. (D) is the trap: it also attacks the label “modest,” but in the wrong direction and for an invented reason (undervaluation). (B) cites passage B’s appraisal problem but runs it backwards.

choices.note: CORRECT. The “standard” is the inventoried population; “leaves out many of the people least able to afford such goods” is the poorest, “whose possessions hardly justified the cost of appraisal.”
Backwards. Passage B says cheap items were often lumped together as sundries; that would make inventories show fewer goods, not more.
Passage B says inventories reflect lifetime accumulation, but nothing about inheritance versus purchase.

Tempting, since it challenges “modest means.” But it goes the wrong way: passage B implies those households were better off than the label suggests, and it never says appraisers undervalued anyone’s goods.
Neither passage discusses the order in which goods spread through social ranks.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A defends a kind of record against criticisms of the sort raised in passage B, and passage B concedes that those criticisms have been overstated.
Passage A describes a body of evidence and a conclusion drawn from it, and passage B argues that the same evidence supports the opposite conclusion.
Passage B rejects the explanation that passage A reports and proposes a different account of the changes in household possessions that the inventories record.
Passage A surveys the uses historians have made of a kind of record, and passage B proposes a method for correcting the biases to which that record is subject.
Passage A presents an interpretation resting on a kind of record, and passage B questions what that kind of record can establish without referring specifically to the interpretation.
questions.explanation: Passage A reports de Vries’s industrious-revolution reading of probate inventories. Passage B argues that inventories are distorted in ways that must be corrected before they can trace changes in consumption, but never names de Vries or his explanation. That is E. C overstates passage B: it doubts the evidence, but it never rejects the interpretation or proposes a rival one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A’s second paragraph; passage B’s first and last paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: What does passage B attack: de Vries, or the evidence? The evidence. It lists three biases in inventories and ends by saying historians must correct for them, mostly with evidence from outside the inventories, before using them to trace consumption. It never mentions de Vries. So: A gives an interpretation built on inventories; B questions inventories in general. (C) is the near-miss: undermining the evidence is not the same as declaring the conclusion false. Unproven isn’t wrong.

choices.note: Passage A never answers criticisms of inventories, and passage B concedes nothing about overstatement.
Passage B doesn’t claim that inventories show ownership falling or flat; it says they can’t be read at face value.
Tempting, since passage B’s points would weaken de Vries’s case. But passage B never says the interpretation is wrong and offers no rival explanation; it only says the evidence needs correcting.
Passage A presents one historian’s use of inventories, not a survey, and passage B proposes no corrective method.
CORRECT. Interpretation built on inventories (A); doubts about what inventories can show, with no mention of de Vries (B).

questions.stem: The authors of both passages would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Goods such as clocks and mirrors became common during the period even among households of quite limited means.
At least part of the rise in ownership recorded in the inventories reflects a genuine change in what households owned.
Probate inventories capture aspects of ordinary domestic life that the personal records of the period seldom document.
The poorest households of the period are underrepresented among the probate inventories that survive.
An inventory’s worth as evidence depends chiefly on how carefully its appraisers assigned values to the goods listed.
questions.explanation: Passage A says few households kept diaries or accounts and that inventories offer “something no other source can”; passage B opens by granting that inventories “record what diaries and account books rarely do.” C states that shared ground abstractly. B is the dominant trap: passage A accepts the rise, but passage B commits only to the possibility that it is partly an artifact and says their distortions must be corrected, largely with outside evidence, before they can trace consumption. D is stated only in passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a view both authors hold.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A’s first and last paragraphs; passage B’s first sentence and last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: For an agreement question, each half of the answer has to be traceable to both passages. Passage B is mostly critical, so look for what it grants: its first sentence says inventories record “what diaries and account books rarely do.” Passage A says the same twice. That’s the common ground. Most students pick (B) because it sounds like a modest compromise both could live with. But passage B never commits to any part of the rise being real; it says the rise “may partly reflect” artifacts and that the records need correcting before they can trace consumption. Hedged isn’t the same as agreed. (D) is a fact passage B states and passage A never touches.

choices.note: Passage A says so, but passage B questions just this: “modest” households in inventories may not have been poor at all.

Tempting, because it’s mild. But passage B never says any part of the rise is genuine; it says the rise may partly reflect who left inventories and how appraisers worked, and that they need outside correction before they can show whether households were buying more.
CORRECT. Passage A: few households kept diaries or accounts, and inventories offer “something no other source can.” Passage B: inventories “record what diaries and account books rarely do.”
Only passage B says this. Passage A never discusses who was left out of the inventories.
Neither passage says this. Passage B’s concerns are who was inventoried, their ages, and what got listed, not the accuracy of the values.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true of the inventories discussed in passage A, would most reduce the force of the concern raised in the third paragraph of passage B?
choices: The average age at death of the householders whose estates were inventoried rose steadily from the beginning of the period to its end.
Within any one decade of the period, the inventories of decedents who died young list such goods about as often as do those of decedents who died old.
Appraisers late in the period were more likely than earlier appraisers to list inexpensive objects individually rather than as sundries.
Many of the inventoried households that owned such goods had members who earned wages by spinning and other piecework, as passage A’s account of the period would lead one to expect.
Most of the householders whose estates were inventoried had died in old age, after decades of acquiring the goods that were listed.
questions.explanation: Passage B’s third paragraph worries that a rise in ownership may reflect a lifetime of accumulation and changes in who lived long enough to leave an inventory, and at what age. If, at any given time, the young and the old dead were equally likely to own the goods, then age at death doesn’t affect ownership, and no shift in the ages of the inventoried could produce the rise: B. D is the trap: it supports passage A’s explanation but doesn’t touch the age problem.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most weakens passage B’s worry about the age of those inventoried.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, third paragraph; passage A, second paragraph (for the trap).

breakdown.analysis: Pin down the concern: inventories record lifetime accumulation by mostly old people, so a rise over the decades might come from a change in who was inventoried and at what age, not in buying habits. That worry needs one hidden premise: older decedents own more of these goods than younger ones. Knock that out and the concern collapses. (B) does it without ever saying “the rise is real,” which is why it’s easy to skip. Most students who miss this pick (D), because it fits passage A’s story so nicely. But a fact that supports de Vries’s mechanism does nothing about whether the rise in the inventories was produced by age. (A) and (E) are about age too, and both point the other way or just repeat the premise.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s about age. But rising age at death would make later inventories hold more accumulated goods, so this makes the concern stronger.

CORRECT. If, at the same date, young and old decedents owned the goods equally often, then how long a person had to accumulate them makes no difference, and a change in the ages of those inventoried can’t create a rise.
This concerns the fourth paragraph’s appraiser problem, and it would make that concern worse: later appraisers listing cheap items separately would create an apparent rise.

Tempting, because it supports passage A’s explanation of the rise. But the question asks about the age concern, and piecework earnings say nothing about whether the rise reflects who was old enough to be inventoried.
This only repeats passage B’s premise that decedents were old. It says nothing about whether ownership depended on age.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that the visit-shortening hypothesis explains bitter nectar better than its rivals do, while conceding that the evidence for it comes from a single experiment
show that experimental evidence has ruled out every proposed explanation of bitter nectar except the hypothesis that it shortens pollinators’ visits
explain why plants whose nectar contains bitter compounds tend to set fewer seeds than plants of the same species whose nectar is sweet
challenge the assumption that nectar functions as a payment offered to animals in exchange for carrying a plant’s pollen
set out one proposed explanation of a botanical puzzle and consider what an experimental test of that explanation does and does not establish
questions.explanation: The passage lists several explanations of bitter nectar, develops one (shorter visits), reports an experiment, and then says what such an experiment leaves open, ending with the point that several explanations may hold at once. That is E. A has the shape of a balanced main-point answer, but the author never ranks the hypotheses; the experiment rules out only thief deterrence at that site, and the last sentence says the explanations need not compete, recasting the question as how much each contributes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage as a whole sets out to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph (puzzle and explanations), the second (one mechanism), the third (the experiment), the fourth (what it leaves open).

breakdown.analysis: Does the author take a side? Look for a verdict. You find only a narrow one: thief deterrence couldn’t have produced this result at this site. Everything else is laid out, not judged: several explanations, one mechanism in detail, one experiment, what the experiment can’t show, and a closing point that the explanations may all be partly true. Prephrase: explain one hypothesis and what the test of it does and doesn’t show. Most students who miss this pick (A), because “argue X, while conceding Y” is the usual shape of a right answer. Here the shape hides a wrong element: the author never says the hypothesis beats its rivals.

choices.note: Tempting: it looks balanced and names the right hypothesis. But the author never ranks it above its rivals; the last paragraph says a single compound might do several of these jobs at once.
Too strong. The experiment speaks only against thief deterrence at a site where thieves were scarce; antimicrobial action, screening, and the by-product view are never ruled out.
Unsupported. The passage says the experiment didn’t count seeds; it never says bitter-nectar plants set fewer.
The payment view is the opening premise that makes bitter nectar puzzling, not a view the passage attacks.
CORRECT. “One proposed explanation” is visit-shortening (one of several listed); “what a test does and does not establish” covers the experiment and the open matters in the last paragraph.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that, in the field study described in the third paragraph, compared with bees on the alkaloid plants, bees on the alkaloid-free plants
choices: left a larger proportion of the visited plant’s own pollen on the flowers they visited
brought pollen from other plants that sired most of the seeds on the plants they visited
