took only a sip or two from each flower before flying on to another plant
left a larger number of the visited plant’s flowers without any pollen at all
caused the plants they visited to produce a greater total number of seeds
questions.explanation: Bees on alkaloid-free plants visited markedly more flowers per plant, and the second paragraph explains that the more flowers a bee visits on one plant, the more of the pollen it leaves on later flowers is the plant’s own. The parentage results fit: a smaller share of those plants’ seeds were sired by other plants. So A. E is the trap: more flowers visited sounds like more seeds, but tracing parentage “does not count them,” and inbred seeds “frequently fail.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what follows about bees on the alkaloid-free plants.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph’s worked example and the third paragraph’s numbers.

breakdown.analysis: Connect the mechanism to the data. Mechanism: eight flowers → most pollen left on later flowers is the plant’s own; two flowers → nearly all foreign. Data: bees on alkaloid-free plants visited markedly more flowers per plant. Outcome: a smaller share of outcrossed seeds on those plants. So bees on alkaloid-free plants left relatively more of the plant’s own pollen. Most students who miss this pick (E), because “more flowers visited” feels like “more seeds.” But the passage says parentage tracing doesn’t count seeds, and self-pollinated seeds often fail. Share isn’t number.

choices.note: CORRECT. More flowers per plant means more of the plant’s own pollen carried from early flowers to later ones; the smaller outcrossed share on those plants shows the result.

Unsupported. The passage says only that a larger share of seeds on the alkaloid plants were sired by other plants; nothing says other plants sired most of the seeds on the alkaloid-free ones, and the mechanism suggests the opposite.
Backwards. That is how bees behave at bitter nectar; bees at sweet nectar work through “flower after flower.”
Backwards again. Skipped flowers are the risk the passage raises for the alkaloid plants, whose visitors leave early.
Tempting, but “Tracing the parentage of seeds does not count them,” and inbred seeds “frequently fail,” so we can’t infer more seeds in total.

questions.stem: The passage mentions each of the following as a matter that an experiment like the one described in the third paragraph leaves unresolved EXCEPT:
choices: whether one group of plants in the experiment was more fruitful overall than the other
whether the compound’s effect on pollinators is the reason the plant came to produce it
whether a plant whose pollinators leave it sooner will have some flowers that receive no pollen
whether a plant growing far from others of its kind gains anything when its pollinators leave early
whether the insects most likely to steal the plant’s nectar could account for the outcome observed
questions.explanation: The last paragraph lists what such an experiment leaves open: seed numbers (A), skipped flowers (C), sparse stands (D), and how the trait arose (B). The likeliest thieves come up only as a point the experiment settles (end of the third paragraph): with thieves scarce, deterring them “could not have produced” the result. So E. The trap is B: its wording is the furthest from the passage, but it restates “Nor does an effect on pollinators reveal how the trait arose.”

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one choice the passage does NOT present as left open by the experiment.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph, with the third for the thieves.

breakdown.analysis: Four of these are things the passage says the experiment can’t settle; one is something it says the experiment does settle. Translate each: 1. “Tracing the parentage of seeds does not count them” = (A). 2. “flowers that departing bees skip may go unpollinated” = (C). 3. In sparse stands a bee may turn to another species = (D). 4. “Nor does an effect on pollinators reveal how the trait arose” = (B). That leaves (E). Thieves are in the passage, which is what makes (E) feel mentioned, but the passage says the opposite: thieves were scarce, so deterring them “could not have produced” the result. Most students who miss this pick (B), because it sounds like a philosopher’s worry rather than a field caveat. It’s the last caveat in the passage. On EXCEPT questions, check the role a mention plays, not just whether the topic appears.

choices.note: Left open: “Tracing the parentage of seeds does not count them.” Fruitfulness overall is the seed count.
Left open, though it’s the hardest to spot: “Nor does an effect on pollinators reveal how the trait arose.” The by-product example spells it out.
Left open: “flowers that departing bees skip may go unpollinated.”
Left open: where plants grow sparsely, a departing bee “might as readily turn to another species,” so early departure may not help.
CORRECT. The thieves are mentioned, but as something the experiment rules out: ants seldom climb the plant, so deterring them “could not have produced it”. That’s settled, not left open.

questions.stem: The passage provides information that most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: Why was the plant used in the experiment well suited to telling the visit-shortening proposal apart from the thief-deterrence explanation?
At what concentration does the alkaloid in the plant’s nectar begin to deter bumblebees from feeding on it?
Does the alkaloid in the plant’s nectar also slow the growth of yeasts and bacteria that would otherwise spoil the nectar?
What proportion of the flowers on the alkaloid plants in the field study received pollen from other plants?
Which insects other than ants are likely to take nectar from the plant studied without carrying its pollen?
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the researchers chose a plant whose likeliest thieves, ants, “seldom climb its stalks.” With thieves out of the picture, an effect of the alkaloid can’t be thief deterrence, which is why the experiment can tell the two explanations apart: A. D is the near-miss: the passage speaks of the share of seeds sired by other plants, not the share of flowers that received foreign pollen.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question the passage gives enough information to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the third paragraph; the numbers at the end of it.

breakdown.analysis: The answer isn’t a quoted fact; it’s a reason you have to assemble. The plant’s likeliest thieves rarely reach it, so if the alkaloid changes anything, thief deterrence can’t explain it; the two explanations then make different predictions. That’s why the plant suits the test. Most students who miss this pick (D) or (C). (D) swaps seeds for flowers, and skipped flowers may get no pollen at all, so one can’t be converted into the other. (C) names an explanation the passage lists, but the passage never says whether this alkaloid does it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Its likeliest thieves, ants, seldom climb its stalks, so the thief-deterrence explanation can’t account for any effect the alkaloid has there.
The study used the alkaloid “at its natural concentration”; no threshold is given.
Antimicrobial action is one of the explanations listed in the first paragraph, and the last paragraph says a compound might do it as well, but nothing says whether this alkaloid does.
Tempting, but the passage gives a share of seeds, not of flowers, and some skipped flowers may have received no pollen.
Ants are the only possible thieves named, and only to say they seldom climb the plant.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the hypothesis that the alkaloid in the nectar of the plant studied benefits the plant by shortening bumblebees’ visits?
choices: Populations of the species that grow in sparse, scattered stands produce markedly less of the alkaloid in their nectar than do populations growing in dense stands.
Bumblebees that encounter the alkaloid at one plant of the species tend to avoid all plants of that species for the rest of the same foraging trip.
The alkaloid is also present in the plant’s leaves, where it discourages grazing by deer and other mammals that feed in the meadow.
In laboratory trials, bumblebees offered only alkaloid-laced nectar for several days came to drink it as readily as they drank sweet nectar.
Nectar containing the alkaloid at its natural concentration supports far less growth of yeasts and bacteria than does nectar from which the alkaloid is absent.
questions.explanation: Shortening visits helps a plant only when a departing bee goes on to another plant of the same species, which the last paragraph says is likely in dense stands and doubtful in sparse ones. If the alkaloid is there for that benefit, selection should favor less of it where it does no good; A reports exactly that pattern. E is the trap: it supports the antimicrobial explanation, and since the passage says the explanations can hold together, it neither helps nor hurts visit-shortening.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports the visit-shortening hypothesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph (the mechanism) together with the fourth (dense versus sparse stands; rival explanations).

breakdown.analysis: What would we expect to see if the alkaloid really earns its keep by shortening visits? Combine two paragraphs. 1. The benefit comes only when the departing bee flies to another plant of the same species. 2. That happens in dense stands; in sparse ones the bee may go to another species, wasting the pollen. So where plants are scattered, the alkaloid costs visits and buys little. A trait kept for this benefit should be weaker there. (A) reports that pattern, and neither thief deterrence nor a leaf-defense by-product predicts it. It looks off-topic at first, since it never mentions bees or seeds. Most students who miss this pick (E), because it shows the alkaloid does something useful. But it’s useful for a different reason, and the passage says one compound can serve several purposes, so evidence for another job is not evidence for this one.

choices.note: CORRECT. The hypothesis predicts more alkaloid where shortened visits pay off (dense stands) and less where they don’t (sparse ones). Finding that pattern confirms a prediction specific to this hypothesis.
This weakens it. If bees shun the species for the rest of the trip, a deterred bee won’t fly on to another plant of the same species carrying the first plant’s pollen.
This fits the by-product explanation from the first paragraph. At most it offers a rival account of why the plant makes the alkaloid; it gives no support to visit-shortening.
This weakens it: if bees get used to the alkaloid, it would stop shortening visits.

Tempting, because it shows a benefit. But it supports the antimicrobial explanation, and the passage says several explanations may hold of one compound, so this tells us nothing about whether visit-shortening is also at work.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: Had the field study been conducted where the plant grows sparsely, the alkaloid plants would probably have set fewer seeds than the alkaloid-free plants.
Had bees lingered on the alkaloid plants as long as on the others, a smaller share of their seeds would probably have been sired by other plants.
In the field study, the alkaloid plants produced a larger total number of seeds sired by other plants than the alkaloid-free plants in the same meadow did.
The alkaloid in the plant’s nectar first arose as a defense of the plant’s leaves and has since been retained because of its effect on bumblebees.
Had the field study been conducted in a denser stand of the plant, bees on the alkaloid plants would probably have visited more flowers per plant than they did.
questions.explanation: The passage attributes the higher share of outcrossed seeds on alkaloid plants to shorter visits, explaining in the second paragraph why fewer flowers per plant means more foreign pollen. If visits had been as long, that cause would be absent, so the share would probably have been lower: B. C is the dominant trap: it turns a difference in share into a difference in number, which the passage says parentage tracing does not measure. D turns the passage’s “could have been” into a claim of fact, and E borrows the dense-stand discussion, which concerns where departing bees go, not how long they stay.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the passage best supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph’s mechanism, the third paragraph’s results, and the last paragraph’s limits.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase; every choice is a hypothetical or a quantity, so check each against what was measured. The experiment measured flowers per plant and the share of outcrossed seeds; the passage explains the second by the first. So remove the shorter visits and you’d expect the share to fall. Most students who miss this pick (C), because a larger share sounds like more seeds. But the last paragraph warns that tracing parentage “does not count them,” and that skipped flowers may go unpollinated. Alkaloid plants could have had fewer seeds in all. A rate isn’t a count. (D) borrows the passage’s by-product scenario but drops its “could have been.”

choices.note: Too strong. The passage says that in sparse stands a deterred bee “might” go to another species; it never compares seed numbers, and “probably” outruns “might.”
CORRECT. The higher outcrossed share is explained by shorter visits (markedly fewer flowers per plant). Take away that difference and the share should drop.

Tempting, since the alkaloid plants had a larger outcrossed share. But that’s a share; parentage tracing doesn’t count seeds, and skipped flowers may have gone unpollinated, so the totals are unknown.
Too strong. The passage offers this only as a possibility (“could have been retained”) to show that an experiment can’t reveal how the trait arose.

Unsupported. Stand density matters in the passage only for where a departing bee goes next (another plant of the same species, or another species), not for how many flowers it works before leaving. Nothing says how dense the study meadow was, either.

questions.stimulus: Folklorist: Some observers claim that the younger boatbuilders of the Tiller coast, who build with plywood and epoxy instead of the oak planks used there for generations, have broken with the coast's tradition. They are mistaken. A craft tradition lives in its designs and its handed-down knowledge as much as in its materials. The younger builders keep the hull shapes their predecessors developed, and most learned those shapes from older builders, so that knowledge has been passed down intact.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the folklorist's argument?
choices: Working in plywood and epoxy has not caused the younger Tiller coast builders to break with the coast's boatbuilding tradition.
The knowledge needed to build the traditional Tiller coast hulls has been passed from older builders to younger ones intact.
A craft tradition consists more in its designs and handed-down knowledge than in the materials its practitioners use.
For generations, Tiller coast boatbuilders built their fishing boats from oak planks rather than from any other material.
The observers who say the younger builders have broken with tradition are focusing on materials rather than on designs.
questions.explanation: The folklorist's point is the unflagged 'They are mistaken': the younger builders have not broken with the tradition (A). Everything after it supports that claim. B is the trap: it is the claim flagged by 'so' at the end, but it is an intermediate step offered to show the tradition continues; C distorts the general premise ('as much as' becomes 'more').

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The observers are mistaken: the younger builders have not broken with the Tiller coast tradition.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A tradition lives in designs and knowledge as much as in materials; the young builders keep the old hull shapes; most learned them from older builders, so the knowledge was passed down intact.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence gives the view the folklorist opposes, and the second, 'They are mistaken,' is the folklorist's answer to it. Everything after that is offered to show the observers are wrong. Don't be fooled by the 'so' at the end: 'that knowledge has been passed down intact' is a subsidiary conclusion. It's one more reason to think the tradition lives on, not the point of the argument. We need an answer that says the plywood-and-epoxy builders haven't broken with the tradition.

choices.note: CORRECT. This restates 'They are mistaken' in full: the younger builders' new materials haven't made them break with the tradition. Every other claim is offered in support of it.

Tempting, because it's the sentence flagged with 'so.' But it's an intermediate step: knowledge passed down intact is one reason to say the tradition continues. It supports the main point; it isn't the main point.
A premise, and a distorted one. The folklorist says a tradition lives in designs and knowledge 'as much as' in materials, not 'more than.'
Background. It explains why anyone would see plywood as a break, but nothing in the argument is offered to prove it.
The folklorist never says why the observers think what they do. This invents a diagnosis of the opponents; it isn't what the argument sets out to prove.

questions.stimulus: Homeowner: Energy auditors claim that adding insulation to a house's attic substantially lowers its heating bills. But my brother had his attic insulated last fall, and his heating bill this winter was higher than it was last winter. Clearly, the auditors have overstated the savings that attic insulation provides.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the homeowner's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that adding attic insulation is the only way for a homeowner to lower heating bills
relies on the homeowner's own report rather than on the judgment of people trained to measure household energy use
fails to consider that a house with a well-insulated attic may still lose heat through its windows and walls
treats one case that seems not to fit a general claim as showing that the claim is exaggerated
takes for granted that energy auditors would profit from persuading homeowners to add insulation to their attics
questions.explanation: The auditors make a general claim about what insulation does; the homeowner rejects it on the strength of one house in one winter (D). C is the closest trap, but heat lost through windows and walls is compatible with the auditors' claim and is not the error the argument makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The auditors have overstated the savings from attic insulation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The homeowner's brother insulated his attic, and his heating bill went up.

breakdown.analysis: One house, one winter. Is that really enough to overturn a general claim? It's like saying: my uncle smoked and lived to 90, so the health risks of smoking are exaggerated. A general tendency allows exceptions, and this 'exception' may not even be one (maybe the winter was colder or fuel cost more). This is the anecdote-versus-general-claim flaw. Know it. We need an answer that says the argument rejects a general claim on the basis of a single case.

choices.note: The homeowner never says insulation is the only way to save on heating. Nothing in the argument depends on that.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our heating bills are high, so we must not have enough insulation.

choices.note: Attacks-the-source answers are usually traps. The problem isn't who reported the bill; it's that one bill can't overturn a general claim.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: My neighbor isn't an engineer, so his report that the bridge sways can be ignored.

choices.note: Tempting, because it offers a reason the brother's bill stayed high. But it doesn't describe what's wrong with the reasoning; heat lost elsewhere is consistent with insulation still saving money.
CORRECT. The homeowner treats one house's bill as enough to reject a claim about what attic insulation generally does. One case can't show a general claim is overstated.
The homeowner never questions the auditors' motives. This describes an argument the homeowner didn't make.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The auditors sell insulation, so their advice can't be trusted.

questions.stimulus:
Hollis: Our town's community garden should assign its plots by lottery each year rather than letting gardeners renew their plots indefinitely. Under the current system, residents who have been on the waiting list for years may never get a plot.

Teresa: But renewal rewards gardeners who spend years enriching their plots' soil. A yearly lottery would hand that soil to newcomers and give no one a reason to improve a plot. The garden should keep its current system.
questions.stem: Hollis and Teresa disagree over whether
choices: some residents have been waiting for years for a plot in the town's community garden without receiving one
gardeners in the town's community garden should be able to keep the same plot from one year to the next
gardeners who have spent years enriching the soil of their plots deserve some reward for that effort
a lottery is a fairer way to distribute scarce goods than a waiting list is
gardeners who receive plots through a lottery would have less reason to improve the soil than current gardeners have
questions.explanation: Hollis wants a yearly lottery instead of indefinite renewal, so he holds that gardeners should not keep the same plot year after year; Teresa wants to keep renewal, so she holds that they should (B). A, C and E are each addressed by only one speaker, and neither compares a lottery with a waiting list (D).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Hollis: switch to a yearly lottery, because people on the waiting list may never get a plot; Teresa: keep renewal, because it rewards soil improvement and a lottery would kill the incentive to improve plots.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Find the one question both of them answer. Should gardeners get to keep their plots year after year? Hollis: no, plots should be reassigned by lottery each year. Teresa: yes, keep renewal. Everything else (the waiting list, the soil, the incentives) is a reason only one of them gives. The right answer won't say 'lottery' or 'renewal'; it describes the same issue in other words.

choices.note: Only Hollis speaks to this. Teresa never denies that people have waited for years; she just thinks the soil argument wins.
CORRECT. This is the renewal question in other words. Hollis: no, plots should go back into a lottery every year. Teresa: yes, keep the current renewal system. Both commit, in opposite directions.
Only Teresa takes a position. Hollis never says soil-improvers don't deserve a reward; he could grant it and still prefer a lottery.
Neither compares a lottery with a waiting list. Hollis compares a lottery with indefinite renewal. Different comparison.
Tempting, because it's Teresa's main reason. But Hollis says nothing about incentives to improve the soil, so we can't say he rejects it.

questions.stimulus: In one farming region, farmers who stopped plowing their fields and instead planted directly into the previous year's crop residue found that, within a few years, their soil held considerably more water after a rain and lost less of it during dry spells. Yet in years with cool, wet springs, these farmers' fields produced smaller harvests than nearby plowed fields did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Plowed fields in the region lose considerably more topsoil to wind and water erosion than unplowed fields do.
Most farmers in the region who stopped plowing did so mainly to cut the fuel and labor costs of preparing their fields.
The residue left on unplowed fields keeps the soil cold in spring, and most seeds sprout poorly in cold, soggy soil.
In years with hot, dry summers, unplowed fields in the region produce larger harvests than plowed fields do.
Soil that holds more water after a rain generally supports a larger population of earthworms, which help aerate it.
questions.explanation: Holding more water sounds like a pure benefit, yet the unplowed fields do worse in cool, wet springs. C explains this: the residue keeps the soil cold, and cold, soggy soil is bad for sprouting seeds, so the extra moisture becomes a liability in exactly those springs. D is tempting because it is about yields, but it describes dry years and leaves the wet-spring puzzle untouched.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: No-till fields hold more water after rain, but in cool, wet springs they yield less than plowed fields.

breakdown.analysis: Why would better water retention hurt? Notice the specific condition: cool, wet springs. In those years more water isn't what the crop needs. We need an answer showing something about no-till fields that hurts the crop specifically when springs are cold and wet. That lets both facts be true at once.

choices.note: Another advantage of not plowing. It makes the lower wet-spring harvests more puzzling, not less.
Explains why farmers switched, not why their harvests drop in wet springs. Motive is irrelevant to the yields.
CORRECT. The residue keeps the soil cold, and wet, cold soil stops seeds from sprouting. In a cool, wet spring the no-till field is both colder and wetter, so it does worse. Both facts now fit.
Tempting, because it's about harvests. But it talks about hot, dry summers. The puzzle is about cool, wet springs, and this says nothing about them.
Another benefit of water-holding soil. It deepens the puzzle instead of resolving it.

questions.stimulus: At the start of this season, one ski area began stationing an instructor at the top of each beginner run to steer novice skiers toward slopes suited to their ability. So far this season, the ski patrol has treated a third fewer injured beginners than it had by this point last season. Clearly, stationing the instructors has reduced injuries among beginning skiers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The drop in injured beginners treated is not entirely due to fewer beginners skiing at the ski area this season.
Most of the injuries that beginning skiers suffer at the ski area occur on runs designated for beginners.
The instructors stationed at the beginner runs are more experienced than most of the other instructors at the ski area.
No other ski area in the region reduced injuries among beginners this season without taking similar steps.
Injuries to beginning skiers are the most frequent and most costly kind of injury that the ski patrol treats.
questions.explanation: The evidence is a count of injured beginners, so it could fall simply because fewer beginners came. The argument needs that not to be the whole story (A); if the entire drop came from fewer beginners on the slopes, the instructors reduced nothing. B is tempting, but even if most beginner injuries happen elsewhere, steering novices could still prevent some.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Stationing instructors at the beginner runs reduced injuries among beginners.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Instructors were stationed this season; the patrol has treated a third fewer injured beginners than at this point last season.

breakdown.analysis: Look at what was counted: the number of injured beginners treated. So what if that number fell? If a third fewer beginners showed up this season, you'd expect a third fewer injuries with no help from anyone. The argument needs the drop to be at least partly something other than a smaller crowd. We need an answer that rules out 'fewer beginners' as the complete explanation.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the drop is entirely due to fewer beginners skiing. Then the instructors reduced nothing; the injury rate is the same, there are just fewer people to get hurt. The conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: The drop in the number of injured beginners treated is due entirely to a drop in the number of beginners skiing at the ski area.

choices.note: Not required. If most beginner injuries happened on other runs, instructors steering people at the top of beginner runs could still prevent some. Negating it doesn't break the argument.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the injuries beginning skiers suffer at the ski area occur on beginner runs.

choices.note: Not required. Ordinary instructors could steer novices just fine. Negating it does nothing to the causal claim.
choices.negation: The stationed instructors are no more experienced than most other instructors at the ski area.

choices.note: Too strong, and about other ski areas. Another area could have cut injuries some other way without telling us anything about this ski area. Negating it is harmless.
choices.negation: At least one other ski area in the region reduced beginner injuries this season without taking similar steps.

choices.note: The argument is only about whether beginner injuries fell because of the instructors. How they rank against other injuries is irrelevant.
choices.negation: Injuries to beginners are not both the most frequent and the most costly kind the patrol treats.

questions.stimulus: Researchers who spent two years observing capuchin monkeys in one forest found that groups whose members spend more of each day grooming one another have fewer violent conflicts within the group than other groups do. A monkey being groomed typically lies still, often with its eyes half closed. Grooming, the researchers conclude, must ease tension among group members and thereby help prevent conflict.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researchers' argument?
choices: Capuchin groups in several other forests also spend a large share of each day in grooming one another's fur.
Capuchins seldom groom monkeys they have recently fought with, so frequent fighting leaves fewer pairs willing to groom.
Some violent conflicts within capuchin groups occur between monkeys that had groomed each other earlier that same day.
The groups in that forest that groom the most are, on average, neither larger nor smaller than the groups that groom least.
Grooming also allows capuchins to remove ticks and other parasites from parts of one another's bodies they cannot reach.
questions.explanation: The researchers infer that grooming prevents conflict from a correlation between the two. B suggests the causation runs the other way: fighting suppresses grooming. C is tempting but only shows that grooming doesn't prevent every conflict, which is consistent with its reducing conflict overall; D, by ruling out group size, actually helps the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Grooming eases tension and so helps prevent conflict.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Groups that groom more have fewer violent conflicts.

breakdown.analysis: More grooming goes with less fighting. But which causes which? Maybe groups that fight a lot just don't groom, because monkeys don't groom their enemies. That's reversed causation, and it's the first thing to check whenever a correlation becomes a cause. We need an answer that shows conflict could be driving the grooming numbers.

choices.note: Other forests grooming a lot tells us nothing about whether grooming reduces conflict. Irrelevant.
CORRECT. If fighting reduces grooming, the correlation is explained in reverse: groups that fight a lot groom less because few pairs are on good terms. Grooming need not prevent anything.
Tempting. But the claim is that grooming helps prevent conflict, not that it prevents every fight. A few exceptions are fine for a 'tends to' effect.
This rules out group size as a hidden factor. That helps the argument, if anything.
Grooming can have more than one function. Removing parasites doesn't stop it from also easing tension. Doesn't hurt the argument.

questions.stimulus: Economist: One town in this region plans to build a large public swimming complex in hopes of persuading young families to settle there. But surveys show that young families here decide where to live mainly on the basis of housing costs and the quality of local schools. So the swimming complex will do little to attract young families to the town.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the economist's argument depends?
choices: Young families in this region give no weight at all to recreational facilities when they decide where to live.
Housing in the town is currently more expensive than housing in most of the other towns in the region.
Most of the young families who already live in the town would use the new swimming complex regularly.
Building the swimming complex will not lead to any substantial improvement in the quality of the town's schools.
The town could attract more young families by spending the cost of the complex on its schools instead.
questions.explanation: The economist reasons that because families choose mainly on housing costs and schools, a pool won't draw them. That works only if the pool doesn't affect either of those factors; if it substantially improved the town's schools, it could attract families through the very factor they care about (D). A is the trap: the argument needs only that recreation matters little, not that it counts for nothing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The swimming complex will do little to attract young families to the town.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Young families in the region choose where to live mainly on housing costs and school quality.

breakdown.analysis: The economist treats the pool and the two big factors as separate things. But what if the pool feeds into one of them? If the complex gave the schools a swim program, a team, a place for physical education, and that made the schools much better, the pool would attract families after all, by way of the schools. We need an answer that rules out the pool working through the factors families do care about. The answer will look oddly indirect: it's about schools, not pools.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the economist's point. But it's too strong. Negate it: families give recreation a little weight. The survey still says they decide 'mainly' on housing and schools, so the pool can still do 'little.' The argument survives.
choices.negation: Young families in this region give at least some weight to recreational facilities when they decide where to live.

choices.note: If anything this would help the conclusion, but the argument doesn't need it. Negate it: the town's housing is cheaper than most. The pool still doesn't touch either deciding factor.
choices.negation: Housing in the town is not more expensive than housing in most other towns in the region.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument is about attracting new families, not about whether current residents would swim.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most young families already in the town would use the complex regularly.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the complex would substantially improve the town's schools. Then it could attract young families through one of the very factors they decide on, and 'will do little' falls apart.
choices.negation: Building the swimming complex will lead to a substantial improvement in the quality of the town's schools.

choices.note: A comparison of alternatives the argument never makes. Negate it: spending on schools wouldn't attract more families than the pool. The pool could still do little.
choices.negation: The town could not attract more young families by spending the cost of the complex on its schools.

questions.stimulus: At Tarrant Freight, a shipment may be sent by express air only if the customer has prepaid the express surcharge for it. Any shipment containing lithium batteries must travel by sea unless it has been inspected by a certified handler. No shipment travels both by express air and by sea. Last week, a shipment for the customer Holloway contained lithium batteries and was sent by express air.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Every shipment containing lithium batteries for which the express surcharge has been prepaid has been inspected by a certified handler.
Every shipment at Tarrant Freight that has been inspected by a certified handler is sent by express air.
Every shipment at Tarrant Freight for which the express surcharge was prepaid was sent by express air.
Holloway's shipment was inspected by a certified handler, and Holloway prepaid the express surcharge for it.
Holloway has prepaid the express surcharge on every shipment it has ever sent through Tarrant Freight.
questions.explanation: Express air requires a prepaid surcharge, so Holloway prepaid it; and since the shipment went by air it did not go by sea, so the lithium-battery shipment must have been inspected (otherwise it would have had to go by sea). D combines both results. A is the near-miss: it generalizes from prepayment rather than from express air, and a prepaid lithium shipment could have gone by sea uninspected. B and C reverse the rules, and E stretches one shipment to all of Holloway's.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Express air → surcharge prepaid; 2. Lithium AND not inspected → sea; 3. Not both air and sea; 4. Holloway's shipment: lithium, sent by express air.

breakdown.analysis: Run the shipment through the rules. Express air → surcharge prepaid (rule 1). Express air → not sea (rule 3). Contrapositive of rule 2: not sea → not lithium OR inspected. It had lithium, so it was inspected. Chain: air → not sea → inspected; air → prepaid. We need an answer that says it was inspected and the surcharge was prepaid.

choices.note: Tempting, because it strings together the words from the rules and Holloway's shipment fits it. But prepaying doesn't put a shipment on a plane; only express air does. A prepaid lithium shipment that went by sea needn't have been inspected at all. True of Holloway, not of every such shipment.
Inspection only removes the sea requirement. It doesn't send anything by air. This invents a rule.
This reverses rule 1. Prepaying is required for express air, not a guarantee of it. Reversing a conditional is the most common trap; watch for it.
CORRECT. Prepaid follows directly from rule 1. Inspected follows because a lithium shipment that wasn't inspected would have had to go by sea, and this one went by air instead.
We know about one shipment. Nothing tells us about Holloway's other shipments. Too broad.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: The Alvaro Foundation recently sold a painting from its collection to raise money for its art-education programs. The painting was donated decades ago by a collector who expressed no wishes about whether it could ever be sold, and the money from the sale will fund programs that serve the foundation's stated mission. Some members of the public object to the sale, but the foundation acted properly.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?
choices: Selling a donated work is proper only if the donor explicitly authorized such a sale at the time the work was donated.
If a donor placed no restriction on the sale of a donated work, an institution that sells the work should spend the proceeds on its mission.
An institution may sell a gift from its collection if doing so breaks no condition the giver attached and the money raised advances the institution's purposes.
Public objection to an institution's sale of a donated work is not, by itself, sufficient reason to regard the sale as improper.
A donor who expresses no wishes about a gift's future gives up any claim to control how the institution uses the gift.
questions.explanation: The ethicist concludes the sale was proper because the donor set no restriction and the proceeds serve the mission; C says, in other words, that those two conditions make a sale permissible. D is the tempting partial match: it disarms the public objection but never says the sale was proper. B uses the stimulus's words but only tells the institution what to do with the money, and A would condemn the sale.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The foundation acted properly in selling the painting.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The donor expressed no wishes about selling it; the proceeds fund programs serving the foundation's mission; some of the public objects.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is 'the sale was proper.' The facts offered are: 1. no donor restriction; 2. proceeds serve the mission. So we want: no restriction AND proceeds serve the mission → sale is proper. Expect it in different words ('gift,' 'giver,' 'purposes'). The public objection is the view being brushed aside, so a principle that only answers the objection won't get you all the way to 'proper.'

choices.note: Opposite. The donor expressed no wishes, so there was no explicit authorization, and this principle would condemn the sale.

Tempting, because it reuses the stimulus's words. But read the arrow: no restriction → spend proceeds on mission. It tells you what to do with the money once you've sold; it never says the sale was proper.

CORRECT. 'Breaks no condition the giver attached' matches the donor's silence; 'money raised advances the institution's purposes' matches the mission. The verdict, 'may sell,' is the conclusion that the sale was proper.
Tempting. It handles the objection the ethicist brushes aside. But showing the objection isn't enough to condemn the sale is not the same as showing the sale was proper. Partial match.
Covers the donor's silence but says nothing about the mission or about whether the sale was proper. Partial match; it never reaches the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Some anthology editors propose that a poem be included in a school anthology only if it was widely read in its own time. But many poems now regarded as central to the literary canon found few readers when they were first published. If the proposal were adopted, then, school anthologies would have to omit many of the very poems that students most need to know. Editors should therefore reject the proposal.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the editor's argument by the claim that school anthologies would have to omit many of the very poems that students most need to know?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the editor's argument, which the other statements are offered to support.
It is an outcome the editor says the proposal would produce, offered as a reason to reject the proposal.
It is a claim that the editor attributes to the anthology editors who favor adopting the proposal.
It is a general principle that the editor uses to evaluate proposals about what school anthologies should include.
It is a consequence of the proposal that the editor offers as support for the claim that many canonical poems found few readers.
questions.explanation: The editor derives this result from the proposal (via the fact that many canonical poems were little read at first) and uses it as the reason to reject the proposal (B). A is tempting because the claim is itself supported, but it in turn supports the final sentence, which is the main conclusion. E gets the role half right but reverses the support relation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Editors should reject the proposal.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many canonical poems had few readers at first; so the proposal would force anthologies to omit poems students most need to know.

breakdown.analysis: Where does the claim come from, and where does it go? It follows from the proposal plus the fact about canonical poems ('then'), and it supports 'Editors should therefore reject the proposal.' So it's a bad result that the editor says the proposal would produce, used as the reason to reject it. The editor doesn't want this outcome; it's the unacceptable result used to sink the rule. A good role answer gets both parts: what the claim is, and what it supports.

choices.note: Tempting, because the claim has support of its own. But it then supports the last sentence. The main conclusion is 'reject the proposal,' and this is the reason for it.
CORRECT. Both parts are right: it's an outcome the editor says the proposal would produce, and it's the reason given for rejecting the proposal.
The proposal's supporters would never say this; it's the editor's objection to them.
It's a specific predicted result, not a general principle for evaluating proposals.
Right role, wrong relation. It is a consequence of the proposal, but the fact about canonical poems supports it, not the other way around.

questions.stimulus: Last year a city's library system began keeping six of its branches open until 9 p.m. on weekdays; every branch had previously closed at 6 p.m. Over the following twelve months, borrowing at those six branches rose by nearly a fifth. The system's director concluded that the longer hours, by letting people who work during the day visit the library, produced the rise in borrowing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Several other library systems in the region have also lengthened the weekday hours of some of their branches in recent years.
Visitors who come to the six branches in the evening tend to stay longer, on average, than visitors who come during the day.
Over the same twelve months, borrowing at the system's other branches, all of which kept closing at 6 p.m., stayed about the same.
Last year the six branches were also the first in the system to receive large collections of newly published books.
The six branches chosen for longer hours were among the system's most heavily used branches even before the change.
questions.explanation: The director credits the longer hours with the rise in borrowing, so the argument is strengthened by a comparison group: branches in the same system, over the same period, without the longer hours, saw no rise (C). That rules out a system-wide or citywide upswing in borrowing. D is the trap: it is about the same six branches, but new books arriving there are a rival explanation, so it weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The longer evening hours caused the rise in borrowing at the six branches.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Six branches began staying open until 9 p.m.; over the next year, borrowing at those branches rose by nearly a fifth.

breakdown.analysis: Borrowing rose after the hours changed. So what? Maybe borrowing rose everywhere that year: a popular reading program, a new city budget, a rainy year. How do you test a cause? Find a comparison group: branches that had everything the six had except the longer hours. If borrowing there stayed flat, the hours look like the difference. Strengtheners often work indirectly like this, through a group the argument never mentions. We need an answer that isolates the longer hours.

choices.note: Other systems lengthening their hours tells us nothing unless we know what happened to their borrowing. We don't.
Tempting, because it sounds like evening visitors are engaged. But staying longer isn't borrowing more, and it says nothing about whether the new hours, rather than something else, raised borrowing.
CORRECT. Same system, same year, old hours, no rise. That rules out a general upswing in borrowing as the cause and points to the longer hours as the difference.
Tempting, because new books are just the kind of thing that raises borrowing. But that's the problem: it's a rival explanation confined to the same six branches. This weakens.
Being busy before the change explains why these branches were chosen, not why their borrowing rose afterward. It's background, and does nothing to show the hours caused the rise.

questions.stimulus: Soil scientist: Nitrogen fertilizer applied beyond what crops can absorb acidifies the soil, harms beneficial soil microbes, and washes into streams, where it feeds algae blooms. Some farmers reply that they apply only what their soil tests call for. But soil tests are sometimes wrong, so any farmer may, in some season, apply more than the crop takes up. Farmers who care about the long-term health of their soil, therefore, should stop using nitrogen fertilizer altogether.
questions.stem: The soil scientist's argument is flawed because it
choices: fails to consider that some farmers may not care much about the long-term health of their soil
draws a conclusion about the health of soil from evidence that concerns only the health of nearby streams
rejects the farmers' reply merely because the farmers have an interest in continuing to use fertilizer
takes for granted that nitrogen fertilizer harms the soil even when crops are able to absorb all of it
treats the chance that a practice will sometimes be overdone as showing that it should be given up entirely
questions.explanation: The scientist grants that the harm comes from excess fertilizer and argues only that any farmer might occasionally overapply; from that risk alone it concludes that fertilizer should be given up entirely, without weighing the risk against the benefits or against ways to reduce it (E). D is the trap: it is the familiar 'excess is harmful, so any amount is harmful' flaw, but this argument explicitly locates the harm in amounts beyond what crops absorb, so it doesn't presume that.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Farmers who care about their soil should stop using nitrogen fertilizer altogether.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fertilizer beyond what crops absorb harms soil and streams; soil tests are sometimes wrong, so any farmer may sometimes overapply.

breakdown.analysis: So what if a farmer might sometimes overdo it? Some drivers sometimes speed; that doesn't mean nobody should drive. The scientist shows only a risk of occasional excess, never weighs that risk against what fertilizer does for the crop, and never asks whether the risk could be reduced. Then it jumps to 'stop altogether.' Careful: you may have seen the 'too much is bad, so any is bad' flaw before. This argument doesn't make it; it admits the harm comes from excess. We need an answer about treating an occasional risk of excess as a reason to quit completely.

choices.note: The conclusion is addressed only to farmers who care about their soil. Farmers who don't care are outside it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Everyone who wants to stay healthy should exercise, so everyone will exercise.

choices.note: The evidence includes soil acidification and harm to soil microbes, not just the streams. Inaccurate description.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The river downstream is polluted, so the farm's soil must be degraded.

choices.note: The scientist answers the farmers' reply with a reason (soil tests can be wrong), not by questioning their motives. Attacks-the-source answers are usually traps.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Farmers profit from fertilizer, so their claims about it can be dismissed.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'excess is harmful, so any amount is harmful' is a famous flaw. But read the argument: it says the harm comes from fertilizer 'beyond what crops can absorb.' Its leap is from a risk of occasional excess to quitting, not from excess to any amount.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Too much salt raises blood pressure, so any salt at all raises blood pressure.

choices.note: CORRECT. The only support for quitting is that a farmer might, in some season, overapply. Treating that occasional risk as enough to abandon the practice entirely, without weighing benefits or ways to reduce the risk, is the error.

questions.stimulus: In a certain region, pottery buried in ancient tombs was usually the finest a family could afford, and much of it has survived intact. Pottery used in everyday life, by contrast, was typically discarded once it broke, and almost all of it survives only as fragments. The region's museums display intact pieces almost exclusively, and most of their visitors take the pieces on display to be typical of the pottery the region's people once used.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: Most of the pottery that the region's ancient inhabitants owned was of poor quality.
Many visitors to these museums probably have an exaggerated sense of how fine the region's everyday ancient pottery was.
Every intact piece of the region's ancient pottery that survives today was originally placed in a tomb.
The museums that exhibit the region's ancient pottery regard fragments of everyday pottery as having little historical value.
Ancient families in the region generally placed in tombs the same pottery that they had used in their daily lives.
questions.explanation: Museums show intact pieces; intact pieces come overwhelmingly from tombs; tomb pottery was the finest a family could afford; and visitors treat what they see as typical. So many visitors likely overrate everyday pottery (B). C is the trap: 'almost all' everyday pottery survives as fragments, so a few intact everyday pieces may exist. A goes from 'not the finest' to 'poor.'

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Tomb pottery was usually a family's finest, and much survives intact; 2. Everyday pottery was thrown out when broken, and almost all survives only as fragments; 3. Museums display almost only intact pieces; 4. Most visitors take the displayed pieces as typical of what people used.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, but chain the facts. Museums pick intact pieces → intact pieces are mostly tomb pieces → tomb pieces are the finest. So the shelves over-represent the good stuff. Fact 4 finishes the job: visitors read those shelves as typical. A biased sample plus people who treat it as representative means a skewed impression. Watch for answers that exaggerate a link ('every,' 'poor') or invent motives.

choices.note: Too strong, and the wrong opposite. 'Not the finest' isn't 'poor.' Everyday pottery could have been perfectly decent. Polar versus logical opposite.

CORRECT. Displayed pieces are nearly all intact, intact pieces come mostly from tombs, tomb pottery was a family's finest, and visitors take what they see as typical. So many visitors likely think everyday pottery was finer than it was. Hedged with 'probably,' which is all the facts need.
Tempting, because it states the chain in its strongest form. But 'almost all' everyday pottery survives as fragments, so a few everyday pieces could be intact. 'Every' goes too far.
We're told what museums display, not why. Their opinion of fragments is never mentioned. New information.
Contradicts the facts. Tomb pottery was the family's finest, while everyday pottery was used until it broke.

questions.stimulus: In a study, researchers asked the parents of 400 kindergartners how often their children engaged in unstructured, imaginative play at home. The children whose parents reported the most imaginative play scored highest, on average, on a test of self-control given at school. The researchers concluded that imaginative play helps young children develop self-control.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researchers' reasoning?
choices: Some of the children whose parents reported little imaginative play also scored very well on the test of self-control.
The test of self-control used in the study has also been given to kindergartners in a number of other countries.
Imaginative play has also been found in other studies to help young children develop larger vocabularies and social skills.
Parents of calm, attentive children were more inclined than other parents to describe their children's ordinary activities as imaginative play.
The parents in the study were not told in advance that their children would later be given a test of self-control.
questions.explanation: The play measure is the parents' own description. D says parents of children who already show self-control ('calm, attentive') label more of their children's activities as imaginative play, so the reported play tracks self-control because of how parents describe it, not because play builds it. A is tempting, but a few exceptions are compatible with an average effect; E removes a possible bias and so, if anything, helps.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Imaginative play helps young children develop self-control.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Children whose parents reported the most imaginative play scored highest, on average, on a self-control test.

breakdown.analysis: Notice where the play numbers come from: parents' reports, not anyone watching. Is a parent's description really a measure of how much a child plays? If parents of well-behaved kids tend to call whatever their kids do 'imaginative play,' the reports would line up with self-control even if play did nothing. That's a measurement problem. We need an answer that ties the parents' reporting to the trait being tested.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a counterexample. But the finding is about averages, and some exceptions are expected. Doesn't touch the causal claim.
Where else the test is used is irrelevant to whether play caused the scores.
Another possible benefit of play. It neither helps nor hurts the claim about self-control.

CORRECT. 'Calm, attentive' is self-control in other words. If those children's parents report more play just because of how they describe their kids, the link between reported play and test scores comes from the reporting, not from play building self-control.
This removes a possible source of bias in the parents' reports. If anything it helps the study.

questions.stimulus: Many people believe that the hospitals with the longest emergency-room waits are the worst managed. But wait times depend heavily on how many patients arrive, and hospitals with strong reputations tend to attract patients from well beyond their own neighborhoods. Moreover, a well-run emergency room treats the most urgent cases first, which lengthens the waits of patients with minor complaints. So a long average wait at a hospital's emergency room ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: is more likely to indicate that the hospital has a strong reputation than that its emergency room is poorly managed
results mainly from the number of patients who arrive rather than from the way the emergency room is managed
is a reliable sign of poor management only at hospitals whose reputations are not strong enough to draw distant patients
does not, on its own, warrant the judgment that the emergency room is badly run
is no more common at emergency rooms that are badly run than at emergency rooms that are run well
questions.explanation: The author pushes back on the popular view by giving two ways a long wait can coexist with, or even reflect, good management. The fitting conclusion is the modest D. A, B and E are near-misses: A ranks the explanations, B makes patient numbers the main cause, and E says long waits are no more common at bad ERs, all of which go beyond 'a long wait alone proves nothing.' C invents a rule for weak-reputation hospitals.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Popular view: longest waits = worst managed; 2. Waits depend on how many patients come, and strong-reputation hospitals draw extra patients; 3. Good ERs treat urgent cases first, which lengthens minor-complaint waits.

breakdown.analysis: The 'But' tells you the author is pushing back on the popular view. Both reasons show a long wait can happen at a well-run ER. That doesn't prove long-wait ERs are well run, and it doesn't tell you which cause is more common. It only shows the wait alone doesn't prove bad management. We need a modest blank-filler: a long wait isn't, by itself, good evidence of poor management. Watch for answers that turn 'can' into 'probably' or 'mainly.'

choices.note: Tempting, because it leans the author's way. But the author never compares how likely the two explanations are. 'More likely' is a ranking the premises don't give.
Tempting, because it borrows 'how many patients arrive.' But 'mainly' is too strong, and the author's second reason, triage, is itself a feature of how the ER is managed.
Invents a rule. The author says nothing about when a long wait does reliably show poor management, and triage can lengthen waits at any hospital.
CORRECT. Both reasons show a long wait can come from popularity or good triage, so the wait alone doesn't justify calling the ER badly run. Modest, and exactly what the premises support.

Tempting, because it sounds like a strong version of the author's point. But the author shows only that long waits can arise at well-run ERs, not that they arise equally often everywhere. Poor management could still make long waits more common. Too strong.

questions.stimulus: School board member: The company that runs our district's school buses has asked the board to raise its payment, citing two cost increases: a jump in diesel prices and higher insurance premiums. But last summer, before diesel prices rose, the company bought at a fixed price all the diesel it will use this school year. And our contract already obliges the district to reimburse the company for any rise in its insurance premiums. The board should therefore refuse the company's request.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the school board member's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If a contractor will itself bear every cost increase it cites in asking for higher payment, its request should be granted.
A contractor should not receive higher payment to cover a cost that its contract already requires the district to reimburse.
A contractor's request for more pay should be refused if it will be left to absorb none of the cost increases it cites.
A contractor's request for higher payment need not be granted if the contractor will not itself bear the cost increases it cites.
Contractors that buy their fuel in advance at a fixed price rarely need higher payments to cover their operating costs.
questions.explanation: The bus company cites two costs: it won't bear the diesel rise (fuel already bought) and it won't absorb the insurance rise (the district reimburses it). The conclusion is a duty to refuse. C bridges exactly that: if the contractor absorbs none of the cited increases, refuse. D is the trap: it has the right condition, but 'need not be granted' only permits refusal; it doesn't make refusal what the board should do. B covers only the insurance cost, and A reverses the rule.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The board should refuse the company's request for higher payment.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The bus company cites diesel and insurance increases; it locked in this year's diesel at a fixed price; the contract already makes the district reimburse insurance increases.

breakdown.analysis: So what does the bus company actually lose? Nothing on diesel (it bought the fuel before prices rose) and nothing on insurance (the district pays that back). Chain: diesel increase → not borne; insurance increase → borne but reimbursed. So: none of the cited increases is left on the bus company. We need a rule that turns that into 'should refuse': absorbs none of the cited increases → request should be refused. Notice the key never says 'diesel' or 'insurance'. 'Left to absorb' is the abstract stand-in that covers both. Most students pick (D) because its condition matches. It fails on the verdict: 'need not be granted' lets the board refuse; it doesn't say the board should.

choices.note: This reverses the idea. It tells us when to grant a request, and the bus company doesn't meet its condition anyway. A rule about granting can't produce 'should refuse.'

Tempting, because it reuses the contract language from the stimulus. But it handles only the insurance cost. The bus company also cites diesel, and this rule says nothing about that. Part of the bridge isn't the bridge.

CORRECT. The bus company absorbs neither increase: it won't pay the higher diesel price, and it's reimbursed for the insurance rise. Plug that in and the rule says the request should be refused, which is the conclusion.
Tempting. The condition fits. But 'need not be granted' only says refusing is allowed. The conclusion says the board should refuse. Watch modal strength: 'may' or 'need not' can't prove 'should.'
So? 'Rarely' is too weak to prove anything about the bus company, and the argument is about whether to refuse a request, not about what contractors usually need.

questions.stimulus: One housewares retailer packs each fragile item it ships in either a molded-pulp insert or a foam insert, choosing between the two at random. In a recent survey, 96 percent of responding customers whose goods had been packed in pulp said the goods arrived undamaged, compared with 91 percent of responding customers whose goods had been packed in foam. So the pulp inserts protect fragile goods better than the foam inserts do.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Among customers whose goods arrived damaged, were those with foam-packed goods more likely to answer the survey than those with pulp-packed goods?
Were the items the retailer packed in molded pulp less fragile, on average, than the items it packed in foam?
Did more of the customers whose goods were packed in pulp respond to the survey than customers whose goods were packed in foam?
Do customers find molded-pulp inserts easier to dispose of than foam inserts once their goods have been unpacked?
Is the percentage of the retailer's fragile goods that arrive damaged lower than the percentage for other housewares companies?
questions.explanation: Random assignment already rules out the obvious confound, that the two inserts carried different goods. What remains is who answered: if damaged foam customers were keener to respond than damaged pulp customers, the gap could be an artifact of response rates (A). A yes weakens; a no strengthens. B is the trap: it asks the confound question the stimulus has already answered. C asks about raw counts, which don't affect percentages.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pulp inserts protect fragile goods better than foam inserts.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Inserts were assigned at random; 96% of responding pulp customers vs. 91% of responding foam customers reported no damage.

breakdown.analysis: First ask the usual question: were the two inserts used on different goods? The stimulus already answers it. Assignment was random. So the remaining weak spot is the word 'responding.' Only some customers answered. If damaged foam customers were more eager to complain than damaged pulp customers, foam would look worse even if both inserts performed the same. We need a question whose answer could go either way: was the response rate among damaged customers different by insert? Most students pick (B) because the fragility confound is the standard worry. It fails because random assignment already handles it.

choices.note: CORRECT. If damaged foam customers responded more readily, the 91 percent understates foam's real record and the comparison falls apart. If not, the survey gap is more trustworthy. Either answer matters.
Tempting, because it's the classic confound. But the stimulus says inserts were assigned at random, so there's no reason to expect the pulp items were sturdier. The argument already closed this door.

Tempting, because it's about the survey. But the comparison uses percentages of respondents, so how many responded in each group doesn't change them. It's the response pattern among damaged goods that matters, not the raw count.
Disposal is a different dimension. The argument is about protection, not convenience. Irrelevant.
Compares the retailer with other companies. The argument compares two inserts within the retailer. Wrong comparison.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the number of deer-hunting licenses issued each year in one state has fallen by about a third, and state wildlife officials expected the annual deer harvest to fall along with it, since fewer hunters would presumably kill fewer deer. Instead, the number of deer reported killed under state hunting licenses has risen steadily each year.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: The state's deer population has grown substantially over the decade, making deer far easier for hunters to find.
A single license now covers every hunter in the license holder's household, whereas formerly each hunter needed a separate one.
Many former license buyers now hunt only on private preserves, which need no state license but must report each deer taken to the state.
Over the decade the state lengthened its deer-hunting season and raised the number of deer each hunter may take.
The state now requires license holders to report every deer they kill, whereas formerly many deer killed under licenses went unreported.
questions.explanation: The puzzle needs something that lets fewer licenses coexist with more deer reported under those licenses. A, B and D do it by raising the kill per license, and E by raising the share of licensed kills that get reported. C explains only the drop in licenses: deer taken on preserves are reported to the state but not under state hunting licenses, so they can't swell the count in question. The reporting clause is the bait.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Licenses issued fell by about a third, but the number of deer reported killed under state licenses rose.

breakdown.analysis: Read the second fact carefully: deer reported killed under state hunting licenses. Fewer licenses, more deer reported under licenses. Two kinds of answer resolve it: something that raises the kill per license, or something that raises how many licensed kills get reported. (C) looks like the second kind, because of 'must report each deer taken to the state.' But preserve deer aren't taken under state licenses, so reporting them doesn't add to the number in question. (C) explains why licenses fell and nothing about why the licensed count rose. Notice the difference from (E): there, the newly reported deer were killed under licenses.

choices.note: Helps. More deer, easier to find, so each license holder kills more. Fewer licenses, bigger harvest.
Helps. Fewer licenses doesn't mean fewer hunters. A household of four now needs one license instead of four, and all four hunt under it.

CORRECT. It explains why fewer licenses are sold, but the deer killed on preserves aren't killed under state licenses, so reporting them doesn't add to the number in question. Tempting to dismiss as a helper because it mentions reporting to the state, but that's the bait. One side only.
Helps. A longer season and higher bag limit let each licensed hunter take more deer.

Helps. The count in question is deer reported killed under licenses. If many licensed kills used to go unreported and now all must be reported, the reported number can climb even as licenses fall. Unlike (C), these deer really were taken under state licenses.

questions.stimulus: Planetary scientist: Some researchers have concluded that the dwarf planet Tavell has no surface ice, because the probe that photographed Tavell last year detected none. But the probe could detect ice only on sunlit surfaces, and near its poles Tavell has deep craters that sunlight never reaches. Moreover, no ice could last on any sunlit part of Tavell's surface. So Tavell does have surface ice, and all of it lies in those shaded craters.
questions.stem: The planetary scientist's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: treats evidence that a negative finding is unreliable as if it were evidence that the opposite of that finding is true
overlooks the possibility that some of Tavell's surface ice lies on parts of its surface that are in sunlight
confuses a condition that is necessary for the probe to detect ice with a condition that is sufficient for ice to be present
draws a conclusion about the whole of Tavell's surface from evidence concerning only the parts of it that are in sunlight
fails to consider that the probe's instruments might have failed to detect ice even on surfaces that were in sunlight
questions.explanation: The scientist shows the probe's null result says nothing about the shaded craters, which undercuts the researchers' 'no ice' conclusion. But it doesn't show there is ice; it only removes a reason to deny it. A describes that move abstractly. B attacks something the argument already handles (no ice could last in sunlight). D is the researchers' flaw, not the scientist's, and E would only weaken the researchers further.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tavell does have surface ice, and all of it lies in the shaded craters.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The probe could detect ice only in sunlight; much of the surface is in permanently shaded craters; no ice could last on sunlit surfaces.

breakdown.analysis: The scientist does good work against the researchers: the probe never looked where ice could hide, so its null result proves nothing. Then comes the jump. 'Your evidence doesn't show there's no ice' becomes 'there is ice.' It's like saying: you searched only the kitchen for my keys, so you haven't shown they're not in the house, so they're in the bedroom. The second half of the conclusion (all of it in craters) is fine, given the sunlight premise. The flaw is the existence claim. Most students pick (D) because it names the researchers' mistake so well. But the question asks about the scientist. Others pick (B), which the argument already answered.

choices.note: CORRECT. The probe's 'no ice' finding is shown to be unreliable for the craters. That's the evidence against ice being knocked down. The scientist then treats it as evidence for ice. Abstract wording, but it's exactly this move.
Tempting. But the scientist gives a reason: no ice could last on any sunlit surface. The argument doesn't overlook this possibility; it rules it out.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The cookies are all in the jar, since I put some there (ignoring the ones on the plate).

choices.note: The scientist never treats sunlight (needed for detection) as enough for ice to exist. Nothing here mixes up those two conditions.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: You need a ticket to get in, and Ana has a ticket, so she got in.

choices.note: Tempting, because this is exactly what the researchers did, and the scientist points it out. But the scientist's own conclusion rests on a claim about the shaded craters, not on sunlit evidence. Right flaw, wrong arguer.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The probe found no ice where it could see, so there is no ice anywhere on Tavell.

choices.note: This would hurt the researchers even more, not the scientist. If the probe can miss ice even in sunlight, its null result is weaker still. It doesn't touch the jump to 'there is ice.'
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The test came back negative, so you don't have the virus (ignoring that the test has false negatives).

questions.stimulus: Every film at this year's Tolland Film Festival that was shot on celluloid was screened at the old Regent Theater. None of the films screened at the Regent was eligible for the audience award. So any film at this year's festival that was eligible for the audience award was not shot on celluloid.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every song on the Larkin album recorded before 1990 features a string section. No song featuring a string section was chosen for the radio edit. So any song on the album not chosen for the radio edit was recorded before 1990.

Every student in Ms. Ortega's class who completed the reading passed the quiz. Some students who passed the quiz did not attend the review session. So some student in the class who completed the reading did not attend the review session.

Every vehicle in the city fleet that runs on diesel is inspected annually. Few of the vehicles that are inspected annually are kept in the north garage. So any vehicle in the city fleet that is kept in the north garage does not run on diesel.

No apprentice in the Garvey workshop is permitted to operate the lathe. Every worker who is permitted to operate the lathe has completed the workshop's safety training. So no apprentice in the workshop has completed that safety training.

Only members of the Marlow Sailing Club who have passed its swim test may take out its sailboats, and no new junior member has passed that test. Hence no new junior member may take out a club sailboat.
questions.explanation: The argument is a valid chain ending in a negative: all A are B, no B is C, so no C is A. E has the same chain in disguise: only those who passed may sail, no new junior has passed, so no new junior may sail. C is the closest look-alike, but its second premise says 'few' rather than 'none,' so its conclusion doesn't follow. A copies the original's wording but concludes about songs not chosen, which doesn't follow either.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Any film eligible for the audience award was not shot on celluloid.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All celluloid films were screened at the Regent; no Regent film was eligible.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; no B is C; so no C is A (equivalently, no A is C).

breakdown.analysis: Map it: celluloid → Regent → not eligible. So celluloid → not eligible, which is the same as eligible → not celluloid. It's valid. Match the skeleton, not the words: you want a valid chain that ends by denying that one group has some feature. Expect the right answer to hide behind different wording ('only,' 'no... has'). Translate 'Only those who passed may sail' into 'sail → passed,' and its contrapositive, 'not passed → can't sail.' Most students pick (C) or (A) because they read just like the original. Check the quantifier in (C): 'few' is not 'none.' Check the conclusion in (A): it's about songs NOT chosen.

choices.note: Tempting, because it copies the original sentence by sentence. But the valid conclusion would be that no radio-edit song was recorded before 1990. Instead it concludes something about songs not chosen, which doesn't follow: an unchosen song could be from 1995. Invalid.
Uses 'some' and draws an invalid 'some' conclusion. The students who skipped the review could be ones who didn't do the reading. Different and flawed.
