Tempting, because it's a near-copy: every A is B, then a negative-sounding second link, then 'any C is not A.' But 'few' isn't 'none.' A few annually inspected vehicles are in the north garage, and those few could all be diesel. One quantifier changed, and the argument breaks.
Flawed. Apprentices can't use the lathe, and lathe users are trained, but that says nothing about whether apprentices are trained. Wrong structure.

CORRECT. New juniors → haven't passed the test; sailing → passed the test (so not passed → can't sail). Therefore new juniors → can't sail. All A are B, no B is C, so no A is C. The wording is reshuffled, but the valid negative chain is the same.

questions.stimulus: A consulting firm asked each of its employees to compare the number of hours he or she works in a typical week with the numbers worked by the firm's other employees, and every employee responded. Most of the employees said they believe that they work more hours in a typical week than do most of the firm's other employees.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Most of the firm's employees are mistaken about how many hours they themselves work in a typical week.
Employees at the firm tend to overestimate the number of hours that they themselves work in a typical week.
Most of the employees who believe they work more hours than most of their colleagues are mistaken about that.
The employees who work the fewest hours at the firm are the ones most likely to be mistaken about how much they work.
At least one of the employees who believe they work more hours than most of their colleagues is wrong about that.
questions.explanation: At most about half of the employees can work more hours than most of the others, yet most employees believe they do, so at least some of those believers must be wrong (E). C is the attractive trap: it reuses the stimulus's wording, but the arithmetic shows only that some believers are wrong, not most of them. A and B go further by locating the error in employees' estimates of their own hours.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every employee compared his or her weekly hours with the other employees'; 2. Most believe they work more hours than most of the others.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase until you do the math. Line the employees up by hours. Someone who works more than 'most of the others' has to be in roughly the top half. So at most about half can truly fit that description. But more than half believe they do. So some of those believers must be wrong. How many? We only know 'some.' 'Some are wrong' isn't 'most are wrong.' We need a modest answer: at least one believer is mistaken. Most students pick (C) because it states the surprising result in its strongest form, in the stimulus's own words. It fails because the numbers force only some believers to be wrong.

choices.note: Too strong, and aimed at the wrong belief. The employees were asked to compare themselves with others; they could know their own hours exactly and misjudge their colleagues'.
Assumes the direction of the error. A mistaken employee could be underestimating colleagues' hours rather than overestimating his or her own.
Tempting, and it's the classic trap here. If 55 percent believe it and 49 percent really are above most others, only about 6 of every 55 believers need be wrong. 'Most are mistaken' doesn't follow.
Plausible, but nothing in the survey tells us which employees are wrong. We don't know this.
CORRECT. More employees hold the belief than can possibly be right, so at least one of them is wrong. Modest and guaranteed by the numbers.

questions.stimulus: Literary scholar: Late in his life, the poet Anselm Rook revised many of his early poems before including them in his collected works, and most readers today know those poems only in their revised versions. Scholars who want to understand how Rook's style developed over his career should therefore study the versions of the early poems that were first published, rather than the revised versions.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the literary scholar's argument depends?
choices: The versions of Rook's early poems that were first published are of higher literary quality than the revised versions.
Rook's late revisions substantially changed the style of most of the early poems that he chose to revise.
Most readers of Rook's collected works are unaware that many of the early poems in it were revised.
Not all of Rook's revisions to his early poems were mere corrections of printers' errors or of factual mistakes.
Rook's style changed more during the early part of his career than it did at any later point in it.
questions.explanation: Studying the first-published versions to trace Rook's stylistic development makes sense only if the late revisions changed something that bears on style; if every revision merely fixed printers' errors or factual slips, the revised versions would show his early style just as well. D says this in negative form. B is the trap: it states the right idea at the wrong strength, since the argument needs only some stylistic change, not substantial change to most of the revised poems.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: To understand how Rook's style developed, scholars should study the first-published versions of his early poems, not the revised ones.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Late in life Rook revised many early poems for his collected works; most readers know only the revised versions.

breakdown.analysis: Why avoid the revised versions? Only because the revisions might hide what Rook's early style was like. That requires the revisions to have touched style at all. If Rook only fixed misprints and wrong dates, the revised poems would show his early style as well as the originals, maybe better. So we need: at least some revisions went beyond non-stylistic fixes. (D) says this in an odd, negative way: not all revisions were mere corrections of printers' errors or factual mistakes. It looks oddly specific, almost irrelevant, until you negate it. Most students pick (B) because "the revisions changed his style" is the prephrase. It fails on strength: "substantially" and "most" go well past what the argument needs. Test both by negation.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The goal is tracing style, not judging quality. Negate it: the originals are no better than the revisions. They'd still be the right evidence of early style.
choices.negation: The versions of Rook's early poems that were first published are not of higher literary quality than the revised versions.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the right idea, but far too strong. Negate it: the revisions didn't substantially change the style of most revised poems. Even if they changed the style of only a few poems, or changed it slightly, the originals would still be the better guide to how his style developed. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Rook's late revisions did not substantially change the style of most of the early poems that he chose to revise.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What ordinary readers know has nothing to do with what scholars should study. Negate it: most readers know about the revisions. The advice to scholars stands.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most readers of Rook's collected works are unaware that many of the early poems in it were revised.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: every revision was a mere correction of a printer's error or a factual mistake. Then the revised poems show Rook's early style at least as well as the originals, and the recommendation has no point. The negative wording hides a simple idea: some revisions touched style.
choices.negation: All of Rook's revisions to his early poems were mere corrections of printers' errors or of factual mistakes.

choices.note: Not needed. Negate it: his style changed just as much later on. Scholars tracing his development would still need the early versions. The argument survives.
choices.negation: Rook's style did not change more during the early part of his career than it did at some later point in it.

questions.stimulus: Every reference librarian at the Whitcombe Public Library speaks Spanish, as do about half of the library's circulation clerks. Some of the library's Spanish speakers work on Saturdays. So some of the library's Saturday staff are reference librarians, and some are circulation clerks.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every trail in Harlan Park is maintained by volunteers, as are about half of its campgrounds. No area that volunteers maintain is open in winter. So no trail is open in winter, and neither is any campground that volunteers maintain.
Every sedan on Corbin's lot has a warranty, as do about half of the trucks on the lot. The vehicle that Ms. Avila bought from the lot has a warranty. So it must be either a sedan or a truck.
Every sonnet in the Kessock anthology rhymes, as do about half of the anthology's other poems. So most of the poems in the anthology that rhyme must be sonnets.

Every canoe at the Tarrow boathouse needs repainting, as do about half of its rowboats. All boats needing repainting will be moved to the dry dock. So some boats moved to the dry dock will be canoes, and some will be rowboats.

Some of the Renfrew print shop's night workers have had fire-safety training. All of the shop's apprentices have had that training, as have about half of its drivers. So the night workers include both apprentices and drivers.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that since all reference librarians and some circulation clerks speak Spanish, and some Spanish speakers work Saturdays, the Saturday staff must include both kinds; but the Spanish speakers who work Saturdays could all be librarians, all clerks, or other staff entirely. E makes the same move with its premises reordered. D is the trap: it copies the original's wording almost exactly, but its third premise says ALL boats needing repainting go to the dry dock, which makes its conclusion valid.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some Saturday staff are reference librarians and some are circulation clerks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All reference librarians and about half of the circulation clerks speak Spanish; some Spanish speakers work Saturdays.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are X; some B are X; some X are L; so some L are A and some L are B.

breakdown.analysis: Does it follow? No. The Spanish speakers who work Saturdays might all be reference librarians, or all clerks, or pages and security guards. "Some X are L" tells you nothing about which X. It's like saying every guard and half the nurses have keys, some key holders came to the party, so guards and nurses both came. Maybe only the janitor did. Look for the same overlap error, not the same words. (E) reorders its premises (the "some" premise comes first) and words its conclusion differently, but the skeleton is identical. Most students pick (D) because it copies the original nearly word for word. It fails on one word: its third premise says ALL boats needing repainting go to the dry dock, so every canoe and the repainted rowboats really do end up there. (D) is valid, and a valid argument can't match a flawed one.

choices.note: Valid. Everything volunteers maintain is closed in winter, so the trails and the volunteer-run campgrounds are closed. No flaw to match.

Flawed, but differently. The warranty holder could be a van or a motorcycle; the argument overlooks other categories. It has no "some X are L" step and concludes about one vehicle, not about a group containing both kinds.
Flawed, but differently. If the anthology's other poems far outnumber its sonnets, the rhyming half of them could swamp the sonnets. That's a proportion-versus-number mistake, not an overlap mistake.

Tempting, because it copies the original almost word for word. But the third premise is "all boats needing repainting," not "some." Every canoe needs repainting and so do some rowboats, and all of those boats go to the dry dock, so both kinds really will be there. Valid, so it can't match.

CORRECT. Reorder it: all apprentices are trained and about half the drivers are trained (all A are X; some B are X); some trained people work nights (some X are L); so the night workers include apprentices and drivers (some L are A and some L are B). The trained night workers could all be apprentices, all drivers, or press operators. Same error.

questions.stimulus: Last winter the price of firewood in one rural region rose sharply. Most households in the region heat their homes with natural gas, and early last winter the price of natural gas rose steeply. Many of these households, facing higher gas bills, probably turned to wood stoves for heat, and it was this added demand for firewood that drove up its price.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Firewood sellers in the region raised their prices as soon as natural gas prices began to climb, before their own sales had changed.
Firewood cutters delivered far less wood to the region's sellers than usual last winter, because an early freeze closed the logging roads.
A larger quantity of firewood was sold in the region last winter than in any of the several winters before it.
Many gas-heated households in the region paid more to heat their homes last winter than they had in any previous winter.
Last winter was the region's coldest in decades, and households that already heated with wood burned far more of it than usual.
questions.explanation: A price can rise because buyers want more or because sellers have less. If supply had shrunk, less wood would have been sold; record sales alongside a record price point to more demand, which is the argument's explanation (C). A is a timing trap: sellers raising prices before their sales changed suggests the rise didn't come from added demand. E is a demand trap, but the demand comes from existing wood burners, a rival to the gas-switch story. D only confirms a premise; B is a rival supply explanation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Added demand from gas-heated households switching to wood drove up last winter's firewood price.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Firewood prices rose sharply; most households heat with gas; gas prices rose steeply early in the winter.

breakdown.analysis: Why else might firewood get pricier? The obvious rival: less wood to sell. Both stories raise the price, so how do you tell them apart? Look at quantity. A supply squeeze raises prices while fewer cords change hands. A demand surge raises prices while more cords change hands. So an answer showing record sales alongside the price spike favors demand. That's (C). It looks like a bland sales statistic until you see the mechanism. Two traps are built to look stronger. (A) ties the price rise to gas prices, but read the end: sellers raised prices before any added buying, which is the opposite of demand driving price. (E) gives you added demand, but from households already burning wood, not from gas households switching. That's a rival cause for the argument's specific claim.

choices.note: Tempting, because it links the firewood price to the gas price in time. But the sellers raised prices before their sales had changed, so the rise came ahead of any added demand. If anything, this weakens the claim that new demand drove the price up.
This is the rival explanation. Less wood for sale would drive prices up with no added demand at all. Weakens.

CORRECT. If prices rose because supply shrank, fewer cords would have sold. Instead more sold than in years. Higher price plus higher quantity is the signature of rising demand, which is what the argument claims.

Tempting, because it fits the argument's story. But it just confirms a premise: gas heat was expensive. It doesn't show those households bought wood, or that wood demand rose. Irrelevant corroboration.

Tempting, because it really is added demand for firewood. But it comes from households that already heated with wood, not from gas households switching. That's a rival source of demand, so it weakens the argument's specific explanation rather than supporting it.

questions.stimulus: Actuary: Last year in one city, 30 percent of the cars involved in accidents were equipped with lane-departure warning systems, even though only 20 percent of the cars registered there have such systems. So it is unlikely that these warning systems make cars any safer to drive.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the actuary's argument?
choices: Drivers of cars with lane-departure warning systems report that the warnings sometimes sound even when the car has not drifted out of its lane.
Lane-departure warning systems cannot prevent accidents that are caused entirely by the drivers of other vehicles.
On average, cars in the city with lane-departure warning systems are driven about twice as many miles each year as cars without them.
Most of the cars involved in accidents in the city last year were cars that had no lane-departure warning systems.
Accidents in the city last year involving cars with lane-departure warning systems were no less severe, on average, than other accidents.
questions.explanation: Cars with the warnings show up in accidents 1.5 times as often as their share of registered cars. But registration isn't exposure. If those cars are driven twice as far, they have about three-quarters the accidents per mile of other cars, which suggests they are safer (C). D is the trap: it's true (70 percent) and sounds reassuring, but it's just the premise restated as a count. A and E, if anything, support the actuary.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lane-departure warnings probably don't make cars any safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Warning-equipped cars are 20% of registered cars but 30% of cars in accidents.

breakdown.analysis: Is share of registered cars the right baseline? A car parked all week can't crash. The fair comparison is accidents per mile driven. Quick math: warning cars have 1.5 times their 'fair share' of accidents (30 ÷ 20). If they're driven twice as far, per mile they have 1.5 ÷ 2 = 0.75 as many accidents as other cars. That flips the conclusion. We need an answer that changes the base rate. Most students pick (D) because 'most accidents involved cars without warnings' sounds like it defends the warnings. But it's just 70 percent, the other side of the premise. Raw counts can't beat a rate argument.

choices.note: Opposite direction. False alarms are a reason to doubt the systems, so this supports the actuary if anything.

Tempting, because it suggests some accidents weren't the warning car's fault. But it applies to every car equally, so it doesn't explain why warning cars show up more often. It doesn't touch the 30-versus-20 gap.

CORRECT. Twice the miles means twice the chances to crash. Adjusted for driving, warning cars have about 0.75 the accidents per mile of other cars, so the data actually point toward their being safer.

Tempting, because it sounds like good news for the warnings. But it's already in the premise: 30 percent with warnings means 70 percent without. Most cars don't have the systems, so most crashes involve cars without them. Count versus rate.
Severity is a different measure, and 'no less severe' gives the warnings no credit. If anything it fits the actuary.

questions.stimulus: Publishing analyst: Sales of the novels published by Ferrand Books fell by nearly a third last year. Some commentators blame a general decline in novel reading, but across the publishing industry as a whole, sales of novels rose slightly last year. So the drop in Ferrand's sales must have been caused by the poor quality of the novels Ferrand chose to publish.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that Ferrand's sales of books other than novels may have risen last year
relies on sales figures from a single year to draw a conclusion about a long-term trend in Ferrand's sales
draws a conclusion about one publisher from industry-wide figures that need not reflect that publisher's circumstances
treats ruling out one possible cause of the drop as establishing that a particular alternative cause is responsible
takes for granted that readers who stopped buying Ferrand's novels began buying other publishers' novels instead
questions.explanation: The analyst rules out one explanation, a general decline in novel reading, and then concludes that one particular other explanation, poor quality, must be right. But many other causes could explain the drop: fewer titles, higher prices, weaker marketing, a lost bestselling author (D). C is the trap: industry figures are exactly the right evidence for ruling out an industry-wide cause, so using them isn't the mistake. E describes something the argument never needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The drop in Ferrand's novel sales was caused by the poor quality of the novels it chose to publish.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ferrand's novel sales fell by nearly a third; some blame a general decline in novel reading; but industry-wide novel sales rose slightly.

breakdown.analysis: The first step is fine: if novel sales rose across the industry, a general decline in reading didn't sink Ferrand. But then what? The analyst jumps straight to 'poor quality.' Why that cause? Ferrand might have published fewer novels, raised prices, cut its marketing, lost its bestselling author, or had trouble getting books into stores. Knocking out one suspect doesn't convict a particular other one. This is a false choice: the argument acts as if there were only two possible causes. It's a classic; know it. We need an answer that says the argument treats eliminating one explanation as proof of another.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument is only about novels. What happened to Ferrand's other books doesn't touch the reasoning about why novel sales fell.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our novel sales fell, so our business is shrinking (ignoring that cookbook sales doubled).

choices.note: The conclusion isn't about a long-term trend. It's about why sales fell last year, and the evidence is about last year too.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Sales fell last year, so our sales have been declining for a decade.

choices.note: Tempting, because using industry-wide numbers for one company is often a mistake. But here the industry figures are used only to rule out an industry-wide cause, and that's exactly what they're good for. The mistake comes later.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Industry-wide, novel sales rose last year, so Ferrand's novel sales must have risen too.

choices.note: CORRECT. The analyst eliminates one explanation (a general decline in reading) and then treats poor quality as the cause, as if no other explanation were possible. Fewer titles, higher prices, or weaker marketing could explain the drop just as well.

The argument doesn't need this. Whether lost readers went to other publishers or stopped buying novels altogether, the reasoning is the same. It's tempting because the rising industry numbers hint at it, but the analyst never relies on it.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our customers stopped shopping here, so they must be shopping at our competitor.
